query.original_query: verbal overshadowing describing degrades non-verbal recognition memory language interference

sub_queries.semantic_query: verbal overshadowing describing degrades non-verbal recognition memory language interference
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the phenomenon of verbal overshadowing, wherein describing a non-verbal stimulus impairs subsequent recognition memory. Our analysis focuses on the role of language interference in disrupting visual representations. Using a controlled experimental paradigm, we compare recognition accuracy for faces and abstract shapes across conditions of verbal description, non-verbal elaboration, and a distractor task. Results show that participants who provided detailed verbal descriptions exhibited significantly lower recognition accuracy compared to control groups, consistent with a retrieval-based interference account. We find that the effect is more pronounced for stimuli with high perceptual similarity, suggesting that verbal recoding disrupts fine-grained visual discrimination. Our analysis further reveals that the degree of interference correlates with the specificity of descriptive language used, supporting the hypothesis that verbal overshadowing arises from a mismatch between verbal and non-verbal representational formats. These findings align with prior work on the cognitive costs of language-based retrieval and highlight the boundary conditions under which describing degrades memory.

sub_queries.semantic_query: verbal overshadowing effect where verbal description impairs non-verbal recognition memory, language interference in visual memory retrieval, eyewitness testimony and verbalization disrupting memory
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the verbal overshadowing effect, whereby verbalizing a visual memory impairs subsequent recognition performance. Participants viewed a target face and, following a delay, either provided a detailed verbal description of the face or completed an unrelated filler task. All participants then completed a forced-choice recognition test. Results indicated that participants in the verbalization condition demonstrated significantly lower recognition accuracy compared to the control group, replicating the classic verbal overshadowing effect. This finding supports the hypothesis that verbal recoding of non-visual information interferes with the retrieval of the original visual memory trace, consistent with a transfer-inappropriate processing shift. The effect was more pronounced for participants who reported using more analytic, feature-based language during description. These results have implications for understanding the cognitive mechanisms underlying language-induced memory distortion and for applied contexts such as eyewitness testimony, where post-event verbalization may compromise the accuracy of lineup identifications.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval in Online Sentence Parsing: Empirical Evidence, Computational Modelling, and Simulations
papers.research_question: How does memory retrieval work during online sentence parsing, and under what conditions does similarity-based interference occur?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Revision Integrated Cue-Based (RICB) model, which successfully predicts similarity-based interference data in floating quantifier processing, emphasizing structural information and revision.
papers.conclusion: The RICB model accounts for the data and underscores the importance of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during real-time sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
Similarity-based interference was observed in ungrammatical sentences but not in grammatical sentences.
The interference patterns were not consistent with existing theories and models.
The RICB model, which assumes heavy weighting of structural cues and includes revision, predicts the observed data.
The results highlight the central role of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during sentence processing.
papers.limitation:
Detecting similarity-based interference requires large sample sizes, particularly in grammatical sentences.
The patterns of interference were not consistent with existing theories and models.
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper reports two experiments (Experiments 1 and 2) and computational simulations designed to investigate and model memory retrieval processes during real-time sentence processing. Central to this study is the hypothesis that linguistic information serves as a cue to retrieve target representations from memory during dependency formation. The basis for this cue-based memory retrieval stems from research showing that non-target representations that match a set of retrieval cues interfere with target retrieval. The susceptibility to this similarity-based interference has been debated in the sentence processing literature, and various hypotheses and models have been formulated and developed. This issue is addressed empirically in Experiments 1 and 2, which investigated similarity-based interference in sentences with a floating quantifier. Bayesian linear mixed models and Bayes factor analyses suggested similarity-based interference. However, the patterns of interference were not consistent with existing theories and models. To reconcile these findings within the framework of cue-based memory retrieval, this paper implements the Revision Integrated Cue-Based (RICB) model based on the ACT–R architecture. This model assumes that structural information is heavily weighted and incorporates the notions of initial retrieval and revision. The results of the simulations indicate that the RICB model successfully predicts the observed data, highlighting the central role of structural information and revision in memory retrieval during real-time sentence processing.

papers.title: The Law of Knowledge Overshadowing: Towards Understanding, Predicting, and Preventing LLM Hallucination
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to knowledge overshadowing in LLMs, can we preemptively quantify hallucinations, why does it happen, and how to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge overshadowing as a key driver of LLM hallucinations, establishes a log-linear law to predict hallucination rates based on knowledge popularity, length, and model size, and proposes the CoDA decoding strategy to mitigate hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The work identifies knowledge overshadowing as a cause of hallucinations, establishes a predictive log-linear law, and proposes CoDA to mitigate hallucinations, providing a principled approach for more reliable LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge overshadowing occurs when dominant knowledge suppresses less prominent knowledge during text generation, leading to factual hallucinations.
Hallucination rate increases linearly with the logarithmic scale of relative knowledge popularity, knowledge length, and model size, following a log-linear law.
This log-linear law enables preemptive quantification of hallucinations before model training or inference.
The proposed CoDA decoding strategy amplifies overshadowed knowledge and significantly improves factuality on benchmarks like Overshadow, MemoTrap, and NQ-Swap.
Larger models exhibit stronger overshadowing due to increased compression capabilities, which can suppress less frequent knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Inability to analyze variables in training corpora of SOTA LLMs like GPT-4o and DeepSeek due to inaccessibility.
Difficulty in accurately quantifying knowledge in large-scale noisy datasets due to language imprecision and ambiguity.
future_direction: Diving deep into model internal representations to better interpret knowledge overshadowing.
Solving more complex and compound knowledge overshadowing hallucinations on larger language models.
Quantifying knowledge in noisy natural language datasets.
papers.abstract: Hallucination is a persistent challenge in large language models (LLMs), where even with rigorous quality control, models often generate distorted facts. This paradox, in which error generation continues despite high-quality training data, calls for a deeper understanding of the underlying LLM mechanisms. To address it, we propose a novel concept: knowledge overshadowing, where model's dominant knowledge can obscure less prominent knowledge during text generation, causing the model to fabricate inaccurate details. Building on this idea, we introduce a novel framework to quantify factual hallucinations by modeling knowledge overshadowing. Central to our approach is the log-linear law, which predicts that the rate of factual hallucination increases linearly with the logarithmic scale of (1) Knowledge Popularity, (2) Knowledge Length, and (3) Model Size. The law provides a means to preemptively quantify hallucinations, offering foresight into their occurrence even before model training or inference. Built on overshadowing effect, we propose a new decoding strategy CoDa, to mitigate hallucinations, which notably enhance model factuality on Overshadow (27.9%), MemoTrap (13.1%) and NQ-Swap (18.3%). Our findings not only deepen understandings of the underlying mechanisms behind hallucinations but also provide actionable insights for developing more predictable and controllable language models.

papers.title: Pierce the Mists, Greet the Sky: Decipher Knowledge Overshadowing via Knowledge Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the origins and internal mechanisms of knowledge overshadowing in large language models during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PHANTOMCIRCUIT, a framework that uses knowledge circuit analysis to dissect the internal mechanisms and training dynamics of knowledge overshadowing in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: PHANTOMCIRCUIT effectively analyzes and detects knowledge overshadowing, offering insights into its mechanisms and a pathway for recovery via circuit optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Higher knowledge popularity (P) and model size (M) cause earlier onset, shorter duration, and quicker recovery from knowledge overshadowing.
Larger dataset size (D) leads to earlier onset but slower recovery from overshadowing.
Knowledge overshadowing dynamics are driven by the co-evolution of subordinate knowledge loss proportion (LP) and relative overshadowing rate (RO).
Attention heads in knowledge circuits that focus on {Xdom, Xsub} are crucial for mitigating overshadowing.
Optimizing the number of edges in knowledge circuits can recover from overshadowing by enhancing attention on key differences.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily rely on synthetic data for controlled analysis, limiting generalization to real-world data.
Applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation is not yet validated.
Dynamic analysis of knowledge circuits throughout training is computationally intensive, hindering scalability.
future_direction: Validate the conclusions on more complex, noisy real-world data and other model architectures.
Explore applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation.
Develop more computationally efficient circuit analysis techniques, such as Information Flow Routes (IFR).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their remarkable capabilities, are hampered by hallucinations. A particularly challenging variant, knowledge overshadowing, occurs when one piece of activated knowledge inadvertently masks another relevant piece, leading to erroneous outputs even with high-quality training data. Current understanding of overshadowing is largely confined to inference-time observations, lacking deep insights into its origins and internal mechanisms during model training. Therefore, we introduce PhantomCircuit, a novel framework designed to comprehensively analyze and detect knowledge overshadowing. By innovatively employing knowledge circuit analysis, PhantomCircuit dissects the function of key components in the circuit and how the attention pattern dynamics contribute to the overshadowing phenomenon and its evolution throughout the training process. Extensive experiments demonstrate PhantomCircuit's effectiveness in identifying such instances, offering novel insights into this elusive hallucination and providing the research community with a new methodological lens for its potential mitigation.

papers.title: Recognition, recall, and retention of few-shot memories in large language models
papers.research_question: What exactly can a language model remember about training examples that it sees only a few times? How long does that memory persist as the model is continued to be trained with new examples?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models can quickly memorize training examples with few exposures, but these memories are rapidly overwritten during continued training, though some residual memory persists. Recognition memory is more robust than recall and exceeds human performance.
papers.conclusion: Large language models are remarkably effective at fast memorization, but retention is a key challenge; improving retention might alleviate issues like hallucination, though perfect retention may not be desirable for generalization.
papers.key_findings:
A single exposure is sufficient for near-perfect recognition accuracy across various stimulus types, even for challenging distinctions like paraphrases.
Recall requires more exposures (typically 3) to achieve near-perfect performance, especially for natural language sentences.
Memory retention declines rapidly in the first few training updates with new data, then more gradually, with some memories persisting even after 100K updates.
Recognition memory is more robust to interference from new training than recall memory.
Memory for natural language sentences is superior to memory for structureless stimuli like random word sequences or random strings.
papers.limitation:
Need to evaluate bigger, more capable models beyond the 13B parameter models studied.
Limited experimental probes of memory, relying only on recognition tests and conditional recall with greedy decoding, which may be too stringent.
future_direction: Investigate whether ideas from continual learning can improve memory retention in neural networks.
Use more fine-grained measures of memory, such as sampling at different temperatures instead of greedy decoding.
Explore how instruction tuning affects memory properties of language models.
papers.abstract: The training of modern large language models (LLMs) takes place in a regime where most training examples are seen only a few times by the model during the course of training. What does a model remember about such examples seen only a few times during training and how long does that memory persist in the face of continuous training with new examples? Here, we investigate these questions through simple recognition, recall, and retention experiments with LLMs. In recognition experiments, we ask if the model can distinguish the seen example from a novel example; in recall experiments, we ask if the model can correctly recall the seen example when cued by a part of it; and in retention experiments, we periodically probe the model's memory for the original examples as the model is trained continuously with new examples. We find that a single exposure is generally sufficient for a model to achieve near perfect accuracy even in very challenging recognition experiments. We estimate that the recognition performance of even small language models easily exceeds human recognition performance reported in similar experiments with humans (Shepard, 1967). Achieving near perfect recall takes more exposures, but most models can do it in just 3 exposures. The flip side of this remarkable capacity for fast learning is that precise memories are quickly overwritten: recall performance for the original examples drops steeply over the first 10 training updates with new examples, followed by a more gradual decline. Even after 100K updates, however, some of the original examples are still recalled near perfectly. A qualitatively similar retention pattern has been observed in human long-term memory retention studies before (Bahrick, 1984). Finally, recognition is much more robust to interference than recall and memory for natural language sentences is generally superior to memory for stimuli without structure.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Prompt-Induced Hallucination in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms driving prompt-induced hallucinations in vision-language models, where models favor textual prompts over conflicting visual evidence?
papers.core_contribution: Prompt-induced hallucinations in VLMs are causally mediated by a small set of attention heads; ablating these heads substantially reduces hallucinations without additional training and shifts model behavior toward visual evidence.
papers.conclusion: Prompt-induced hallucinations are a mechanistically localized and model-dependent failure mode in VLMs, and targeted interventions like attention head ablation can improve visual grounding under prompt-image mismatches.
papers.key_findings:
PIH occurs more frequently as the number of objects in an image increases, and models are more likely to conform to the prompt when their visual confidence is low.
A small subset of attention heads (PIH-heads) is causally responsible for propagating prompt-induced numerical errors; ablating these heads reduces PIH by at least 40% without degrading general counting performance.
PIH-heads are often located in early layers and are shared across models with the same language backbone, indicating they originate from the language model rather than vision-specific components.
Ablation of PIH-heads generalizes beyond counting to a color identification task, reducing prompt-color copying by up to 94.25%.
PIH-head ablation consistently reduces prompt copying and increases attention mass to image tokens, though the specific implementation of copying suppression varies across models.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on medium-scale VLMs (~7B parameters), and the identified PIH heads and ablation effects may not generalize directly to substantially larger models.
The analysis relies on attention-based methods, which offer only a partial view of internal computation, and heads with strong behavioral influence may not exhibit clear or human-aligned attention patterns.
Ablating PIH heads may induce secondary changes in the behavior of other attention heads or layers, which are not traced in this work.
The exact mechanism by which PIH ablation reduces copying differs across models (e.g., encouraging format copying in Qwen-VL while decreasing it in Janus-Pro) and is not fully understood.
future_direction: Determining the exact mechanism as to why PIH ablations cause different forms of copying reduction across models.
Developing a better understanding of whether differences are due to architecture, patterns in selected heads, or training data to give a more complete picture of prompt-induced hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs) are highly capable, yet often hallucinate by favoring textual prompts over visual evidence. We study this failure mode in a controlled object-counting setting, where the prompt overstates the number of objects in the image (e.g., asking a model to describe four waterlilies when only three are present). At low object counts, models often correct the overestimation, but as the number of objects increases, they increasingly conform to the prompt regardless of the discrepancy. Through mechanistic analysis of three VLMs, we identify a small set of attention heads whose ablation substantially reduces prompt-induced hallucinations (PIH) by at least 40% without additional training. Across models, PIH-heads mediate prompt copying in model-specific ways. We characterize these differences and show that PIH ablation increases correction toward visual evidence. Our findings offer insights into the internal mechanisms driving prompt-induced hallucinations, revealing model-specific differences in how these behaviors are implemented.

papers.title: A Language Model with Limited Memory Capacity Captures Interference in Human Sentence Processing
papers.research_question: Can a neural language model with limited memory capacity (single self-attention head) capture similarity-based interference effects (semantic and syntactic) observed in human sentence processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a recurrent neural language model with a single self-attention head (CBR-RNN) that integrates expectation and memory-based theories of sentence processing, and shows that its attention mechanism captures semantic and syntactic interference effects observed in human experiments.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that mechanistic explanations of processing difficulty rooted in memory retrieval constraints can emerge as a by-product of minimizing the surprisal of upcoming words in a language model with limited memory capacity.
papers.key_findings:
The CBR-RNN's single attention head tracks subject-verb dependencies over long distances and with intervening nouns, without direct supervision.
The model captures both agreement attraction and semantic attraction effects, as measured by relative attention and surprisal.
In double violation conditions, the effects of agreement and semantic attraction are additive, consistent with human data.
Surprisal estimates from the model also capture the attraction effects, providing a unified account of expectation and memory-based processing difficulty.
Compared to GPT-2, which requires identifying specialized attention heads, the single-head model provides a simpler and more cognitively plausible measure of interference.
papers.limitation:
Only subject-verb dependencies were investigated; other dependency types (e.g., reflexive anaphora, filler-gap) remain for future work.
The model assumes working memory items are representations of previous timesteps, whereas cue-based retrieval theories typically assume syntactic constituents.
It is unclear whether the model learns interpretable linguistic features (e.g., [+/-subject]) that are posited by cognitive theories.
Training data is Wikipedia text, which is not developmentally plausible and lacks multimodal experience.
future_direction: Evaluate the model on various dependency types, such as reflexive anaphora and filler-gap dependencies.
Incorporate syntactic attention masking to explicitly represent syntactic structure in memory.
Investigate whether training on developmentally-plausible corpora (e.g., child-directed speech) leads to more humanlike memory retrieval behaviors.
papers.abstract: Two of the central factors believed to underpin human sentence processing difficulty are expectations and retrieval from working memory. A recent attempt to create a unified cognitive model integrating these two factors have relied on the parallels between the self-attention mechanism of transformer language models and cue-based retrieval theories of working memory in human sentence processing (Ryu and Lewis 2021). While the authors show that attention patterns in specialized attention heads of GPT-2 are consistent with a key prediction of cue-based retrieval models, similarity-based interference effects, their method requires the identification of syntactically specialized attention heads, and makes an cognitively implausible implicit assumption that hundreds of memory retrieval operations take place in parallel. In the present work, we develop a recurrent neural language model with a single self-attention head, which more closely parallels the memory system assumed by cognitive theories. We show that our model's single attention head can capture semantic and syntactic interference effects observed in human experiments.

papers.title: Episodic grammar: a computational model of the interaction between episodic and semantic memory in language processing
papers.research_question: How do episodic and semantic memory interact in language processing, and can this be modeled computationally for syntactic parsing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an episodic grammar model that integrates semantic and episodic memory for syntactic parsing, achieving competitive performance on the WSJ corpus.
papers.conclusion: The episodic grammar framework unifies rule-based and exemplar-based approaches to syntax within a neural perspective, interpreting them as semantic and episodic memory respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The episodic grammar model improves parsing performance over baseline PCFG models.
Left-corner derivation strategy outperforms top-down derivation in the episodic framework.
Including discontiguous episodes provides minor improvements in F-score.
The model's performance is robust across different n-best list sizes for reranking.
Episodic grammar offers a content-addressable memory approach that avoids large grammar sizes.
papers.limitation: Reranking has limitations as an assessment of the model's performance due to upper and lower bound precision and recall scores from the third-party parser.
future_direction: Developing a full episodic chart parser that computes parse probabilities online via spreading activation.
Integrating the model with the HPN network in a connectionist framework for unsupervised learning.
Investigating syntactic priming effects and recency effects in sentence processing.
papers.abstract: We present a model of the interaction of semantic and episodic memory in language processing. Our work shows how language processing can be understood in terms of memory retrieval. We point out that the perceived dichotomy between rule-based versus exemplar-based language modelling can be interpreted in a neuro-biological perspective in terms of the interaction between a semantic memory system that encodes linguistic knowledge in the form of abstract rules, and an episodic memory that stores concrete linguistic events. We implement the idea of a semantic-episodic memory integration in a probabilistic grammar, and evaluate its performance as a syntactic parser on corpora of natural language. Our labeled precision and recall results are competitive with state-of-the-art syntactic parsers, with F-scores up to 90.68 on section 22 of the Penn WSJ corpus.

papers.title: DeCAF: A Deep Convolutional Activation Feature for Generic Visual Recognition
papers.research_question: Whether features extracted from the activation of a deep convolutional network trained on a large, fixed set of object recognition tasks can be repurposed to novel generic visual recognition tasks.
papers.core_contribution: Features extracted from a deep convolutional network trained on ImageNet (DeCAF) serve as a powerful, generic visual representation that outperforms traditional hand-engineered features on a variety of recognition tasks when used with simple linear classifiers.
papers.conclusion: Deep convolutional activation features learned from a large labeled object database can be successfully repurposed for a wide spectrum of visual recognition tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance with simple linear classifiers.
papers.key_findings:
Features from deeper layers (DeCAF6, DeCAF7) perform better than earlier layers for transfer tasks.
Applying dropout regularization to the features improves classification performance.
DeCAF features significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods on Caltech-101, Office domain adaptation, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and SUN-397 datasets.
Visualizations using t-SNE show that DeCAF features cluster images semantically, even for categories not seen during training.
The features demonstrate robustness to domain shifts, effectively clustering same-category instances across different domains in the Office dataset.
future_direction: Application of DeCAF to detection, retrieval, and category discovery settings.
Exploring sparse approaches like Bayesian output coding for classification into larger numbers of object categories.
papers.abstract: We evaluate whether features extracted from the activation of a deep convolutional network trained in a fully supervised fashion on a large, fixed set of object recognition tasks can be re-purposed to novel generic tasks. Our generic tasks may differ significantly from the originally trained tasks and there may be insufficient labeled or unlabeled data to conventionally train or adapt a deep architecture to the new tasks. We investigate and visualize the semantic clustering of deep convolutional features with respect to a variety of such tasks, including scene recognition, domain adaptation, and fine-grained recognition challenges. We compare the efficacy of relying on various network levels to define a fixed feature, and report novel results that significantly outperform the state-of-the-art on several important vision challenges. We are releasing DeCAF, an open-source implementation of these deep convolutional activation features, along with all associated network parameters to enable vision researchers to be able to conduct experimentation with deep representations across a range of visual concept learning paradigms.

papers.title: Visualizing and Understanding Convolutional Networks
papers.research_question: Why do large convolutional network models perform so well on image classification, and how can they be improved?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel visualization technique using a deconvolutional network to understand intermediate feature layers and the classifier operation in convolutional networks, which is used diagnostically to improve model architecture and achieve better performance on ImageNet.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a visualization technique that provides insight into the internal workings of convnets, enabling model improvement and demonstrating the importance of depth, while also showing the strong generalization capability of ImageNet-trained features to other datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Visualizations reveal that features become more compositional, invariant, and class-discriminative in higher layers of the network.
Visualizations helped identify architectural problems (large stride and filter size in first layer), leading to an improved model that outperforms Krizhevsky et al. on ImageNet.
Occlusion experiments show the model is sensitive to local object structure and does not rely solely on broad scene context for classification.
Ablation studies demonstrate that network depth is vital for performance, not any individual layer.
Features from an ImageNet-trained convnet generalize well to other datasets (Caltech-101, Caltech-256) when only the softmax classifier is retrained.
papers.limitation:
The visualization approach only visualizes a single activation at a time, not the joint activity present in a layer.
The convnet model generalized less well to PASCAL VOC data, possibly due to dataset bias.
future_direction: Using a different loss function that permits multiple objects per image to improve performance on datasets like PASCAL and enable object detection.

papers.title: Erased or Dormant? Rethinking Concept Erasure Through Reversibility
papers.research_question: To what extent do concept erasure techniques in diffusion models truly remove, rather than merely suppress, targeted concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that existing concept erasure methods only suppress concepts and do not remove them, as they can be easily recovered with minimal parameter adaptation.
papers.conclusion: Concept erasure methods are reversible and only suppress concepts, not remove them, calling for a rethinking of erasure towards more irreversible methods.
papers.key_findings:
Erased concepts can be recovered with high fidelity using lightweight parameter adaptation.
This reversibility is consistent across six erasure methods, multiple concept types, and different diffusion backbones.
Theoretical analysis shows that reversed weights remain bounded to original parameters, indicating that representations persist.
Current erasure methods achieve only conditional suppression, not permanent removal.
The paper calls for more robust erasure methods that dismantle latent structures.
future_direction: Develop erasure strategies that explicitly dismantle residual representations and provide stronger guarantees of irreversibility
Establish more rigorous standards for evaluating safety in generative models
papers.abstract: To what extent does concept erasure eliminate generative capacity in diffusion models? While prior evaluations have primarily focused on measuring concept suppression under specific textual prompts, we explore a complementary and fundamental question: do current concept erasure techniques genuinely remove the ability to generate targeted concepts, or do they merely achieve superficial, prompt-specific suppression? We systematically evaluate the robustness and reversibility of two representative concept erasure methods, Unified Concept Editing and Erased Stable Diffusion, by probing their ability to eliminate targeted generative behaviors in text-to-image models. These methods attempt to suppress undesired semantic concepts by modifying internal model parameters, either through targeted attention edits or model-level fine-tuning strategies. To rigorously assess whether these techniques truly erase generative capacity, we propose an instance-level evaluation strategy that employs lightweight fine-tuning to explicitly test the reactivation potential of erased concepts. Through quantitative metrics and qualitative analyses, we show that erased concepts often reemerge with substantial visual fidelity after minimal adaptation, indicating that current methods suppress latent generative representations without fully eliminating them. Our findings reveal critical limitations in existing concept erasure approaches and highlight the need for deeper, representation-level interventions and more rigorous evaluation standards to ensure genuine, irreversible removal of concepts from generative models.

papers.title: Language-biased image classification: evaluation based on semantic representations
papers.research_question: Does language-biased image classification in artificial models like CLIP depend on shared semantic representations between words and images, similar to human picture-word interference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to evaluate language-biased image classification in joint vision-language models and finds that CLIP exhibits language bias but without shared semantic representations between words and images.
papers.conclusion: CLIP acquires the ability to recognize visual word forms but does not acquire shared semantic representations for words and images, and the benchmark enables step-by-step evaluation of semantic interactions in joint language-vision learning.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP shows high label switching rates when words are superimposed on images, indicating strong language bias.
The bias occurs even across different category levels (superordinate vs basic).
The bias does not depend on semantic similarity between image and word categories.
Representational similarity analysis shows that word representations in CLIP are not shared with image representations.
The bias is robust to different prompts but can be reduced by explicitly describing the superimposed word in the prompt.
papers.limitation: The study does not investigate how CLIP acquires the biased representations or the role of potential biases in the training data.
future_direction: Investigate how CLIP acquires biased representations and the role of training data biases.
Make biases more human-like by controlling joint learning curricula of language and vision.
papers.abstract: Humans show language-biased image recognition for a word-embedded image, known as picture-word interference. Such interference depends on hierarchical semantic categories and reflects that human language processing highly interacts with visual processing. Similar to humans, recent artificial models jointly trained on texts and images, e.g., OpenAI CLIP, show language-biased image classification. Exploring whether the bias leads to interference similar to those observed in humans can contribute to understanding how much the model acquires hierarchical semantic representations from joint learning of language and vision. The present study introduces methodological tools from the cognitive science literature to assess the biases of artificial models. Specifically, we introduce a benchmark task to test whether words superimposed on images can distort the image classification across different category levels and, if it can, whether the perturbation is due to the shared semantic representation between language and vision. Our dataset is a set of word-embedded images and consists of a mixture of natural image datasets and hierarchical word labels with superordinate/basic category levels. Using this benchmark test, we evaluate the CLIP model. We show that presenting words distorts the image classification by the model across different category levels, but the effect does not depend on the semantic relationship between images and embedded words. This suggests that the semantic word representation in the CLIP visual processing is not shared with the image representation, although the word representation strongly dominates for word-embedded images.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Model Organisms for Human Associative Learning
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit representational dynamics akin to human associative learning, and can they help disambiguate between competing hypotheses for representational change? How does vocabulary interference modulate representational change?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs exhibit a non-monotonic pattern of representational change during associative learning (consistent with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis), and this change is modulated by vocabulary interference, with higher interference leading to stronger differentiation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can serve as accessible and general computational models for studying human associative learning, providing new insights into how local pair similarity and global competition shape representational change.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show three distinct phases of learning during in-context associative learning: encoding (accuracy increases), consolidation (accuracy stabilizes), and forgetting (accuracy declines).
During the consolidation phase, moderately similar token pairs significantly differentiate, producing a U-shaped pattern of representational change that aligns with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis.
Vocabulary interference—the similarity between a paired item and the model's prior knowledge—modulates representational change: higher interference leads to stronger differentiation.
The non-monotonic differentiation pattern is only present during consolidation and disappears during encoding and forgetting phases.
These representational dynamics are consistent across six different open-source LLMs, despite architectural differences.
papers.limitation:
The token pairs used are synthetic and optimized for similarity, which may not reflect naturalistic learning scenarios.
The forgetting phase is not well understood, and its causes require further investigation.
LLMs are not biologically plausible models of the brain, limiting direct comparisons to neural mechanisms.
future_direction: Investigating the causes of forgetting and predicting when it occurs.
Extending the analysis to more naturalistic stimuli and real-world associative learning tasks.
Exploring how different model architectures (e.g., with explicit memory modules) affect representational dynamics.
papers.abstract: Associative learning--forming links between co-occurring items--is fundamental to human cognition, reshaping internal representations in complex ways. Testing hypotheses on how representational changes occur in biological systems is challenging, but large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable alternative. Building on LLMs' in-context learning, we adapt a cognitive neuroscience associative learning paradigm and investigate how representations evolve across six models. Our initial findings reveal a non-monotonic pattern consistent with the Non-Monotonic Plasticity Hypothesis, with moderately similar items differentiating after learning. Leveraging the controllability of LLMs, we further show that this differentiation is modulated by the overlap of associated items with the broader vocabulary--a factor we term vocabulary interference, capturing how new associations compete with prior knowledge. We find that higher vocabulary interference amplifies differentiation, suggesting that representational change is influenced by both item similarity and global competition. Our findings position LLMs not only as powerful tools for studying representational dynamics in human-like learning systems, but also as accessible and general computational models for generating new hypotheses about the principles underlying memory reorganization in the brain.

papers.title: Show, Attend and Tell: Neural Image Caption Generation with Visual Attention
papers.research_question: How can attention mechanisms be incorporated into neural networks for image caption generation to allow the model to dynamically focus on salient parts of an image while generating corresponding words?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces an attention-based model for image caption generation that learns to align image regions with generated words, achieving state-of-the-art performance and providing interpretability through attention visualizations.
papers.conclusion: The attention-based approach provides state-of-the-art performance on image caption generation benchmarks and offers interpretability by visualizing where the model focuses when generating words, with potential applications in other domains using the encoder-decoder framework.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed soft and hard attention models achieve state-of-the-art performance on the Flickr8k, Flickr30k, and MS COCO benchmark datasets.
The attention mechanism allows the model to learn interpretable alignments between image regions and generated words, which can be visualized.
The soft attention model is differentiable and trainable with standard backpropagation, while the hard attention model is trained using a stochastic variational lower bound and REINFORCE.
Using attention with lower-level convolutional features (instead of a single static representation) enables richer, more descriptive captions.
A doubly stochastic regularization on the attention weights encourages the model to pay attention to every part of the image over the generation process, improving BLEU scores.
papers.abstract: Inspired by recent work in machine translation and object detection, we introduce an attention based model that automatically learns to describe the content of images. We describe how we can train this model in a deterministic manner using standard backpropagation techniques and stochastically by maximizing a variational lower bound. We also show through visualization how the model is able to automatically learn to fix its gaze on salient objects while generating the corresponding words in the output sequence. We validate the use of attention with state-of-the-art performance on three benchmark datasets: Flickr8k, Flickr30k and MS COCO.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: How transferable are features in deep neural networks?
papers.research_question: How transferable are features in deep neural networks? Specifically, how general or specific are features in different layers, and what factors affect transferability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper quantifies the transferability of features in deep neural networks, showing that transferability is affected by both feature specificity and co-adaptation of neurons, and that initializing with transferred features can improve generalization even after fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Features in deep neural networks transition from general to specific across layers, and transferring features can improve generalization performance even after fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transferability is negatively affected by two distinct issues: the specialization of higher layer neurons to the original task and optimization difficulties due to splitting co-adapted neurons.
The transferability of features decreases as the distance between the base task and target task increases.
Transferring features from even distant tasks is better than using random features.
Initializing a network with transferred features from almost any number of layers can produce a boost to generalization that lingers even after fine-tuning to the target dataset.
papers.abstract: Many deep neural networks trained on natural images exhibit a curious phenomenon in common: on the first layer they learn features similar to Gabor filters and color blobs. Such first-layer features appear not to be specific to a particular dataset or task, but general in that they are applicable to many datasets and tasks. Features must eventually transition from general to specific by the last layer of the network, but this transition has not been studied extensively. In this paper we experimentally quantify the generality versus specificity of neurons in each layer of a deep convolutional neural network and report a few surprising results. Transferability is negatively affected by two distinct issues: (1) the specialization of higher layer neurons to their original task at the expense of performance on the target task, which was expected, and (2) optimization difficulties related to splitting networks between co-adapted neurons, which was not expected. In an example network trained on ImageNet, we demonstrate that either of these two issues may dominate, depending on whether features are transferred from the bottom, middle, or top of the network. We also document that the transferability of features decreases as the distance between the base task and target task increases, but that transferring features even from distant tasks can be better than using random features. A final surprising result is that initializing a network with transferred features from almost any number of layers can produce a boost to generalization that lingers even after fine-tuning to the target dataset.

papers.title: Memory in humans and deep language models: Linking hypotheses for model augmentation
papers.research_question: How can insights from human memory inform memory augmentation in Transformers, and can surprisal serve as a linking hypothesis for memory encoding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for integrating human memory insights into memory-augmented Transformers via linking hypotheses, and demonstrates that surprisal from GPT-2 predicts human memory performance in a narrative recall task.
papers.conclusion: Surprisal is a viable candidate for an encoding policy in memory-augmented Transformers, and linking hypotheses provide a principled way to integrate human memory insights into AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Word surprisal from GPT-2 inversely correlates with cloze task performance, indicating that surprising words predict lower performance regardless of prior exposure.
Word surprisal positively correlates with the memory effect (improvement due to story exposure), suggesting that surprisal can predict human memory for narratives.
The correlation between surprisal and memory effect improves with longer context windows and plateaus around 600 tokens.
Attention weights from GPT-2 layers show weak or no correlation with memory performance, suggesting that attention may not be a strong predictor of memory in this context.
In a multiple regression, word surprisal, distinctiveness, and word frequency all significantly predict memory performance, with word frequency having the largest negative effect.
papers.limitation:
The story used only consisted of 1033 tokens, which only exceeds the input size of GPT-2 by a small margin, limiting the evaluation of long-range dependencies.
The evaluation used a cloze task; naturalistic free-recall data would provide a more ecologically valid benchmark.
The study only evaluated surprisal; a more comprehensive evaluation of surprisal-related measures is needed.
future_direction: Using texts that significantly exceed 1024 tokens to better address temporal generalization limits in Transformer models.
Evaluating model performance on naturalistic free-recall data for more ecological validity.
More comprehensive evaluation of surprisal-related measures generated using Transformer outputs or parameter states.
papers.abstract: The computational complexity of the self-attention mechanism in Transformer models significantly limits their ability to generalize over long temporal durations. Memory-augmentation, or the explicit storing of past information in external memory for subsequent predictions, has become a constructive avenue for mitigating this limitation. We argue that memory-augmented Transformers can benefit substantially from considering insights from the memory literature in humans. We detail an approach for integrating evidence from the human memory system through the specification of cross-domain linking hypotheses. We then provide an empirical demonstration to evaluate the use of surprisal as a linking hypothesis, and further identify the limitations of this approach to inform future research.

papers.title: Amnesic Probing: Behavioral Explanation with Amnesic Counterfactuals
papers.research_question: Does high probing performance indicate that the probed information is actually used by the model for prediction? The paper aims to assess the importance of a property for a task by removing it and measuring the behavioral change.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Amnesic Probing, a counterfactual method to assess the importance of a property for a task by removing it from the representation and measuring the behavioral change. Shows that high probing performance does not necessarily mean the property is used by the model.
papers.conclusion: Amnesic probing provides a richer view of how linguistic information is used by neural models compared to conventional probing, and calls for increased scrutiny of claims based on probing results.
papers.key_findings:
High probing performance does not correlate with task importance.
Some properties (like dependency and POS) are important for word prediction, while others (like phrase boundaries) are not.
The importance of properties differs between masked and non-masked settings.
Different labels within a property (e.g., different POS tags) have different impacts on word prediction.
The recovery of properties after removal varies across layers.
papers.limitation:
The method only removes linearly-present information, and the representation of properties might be intertwined.
The selectivity control is not perfect, and the intervention may remove more information than intended.
future_direction: Develop non-linear removal methods.
Further investigate the relative importance of different properties.
papers.abstract: A growing body of work makes use of probing to investigate the working of neural models, often considered black boxes. Recently, an ongoing debate emerged surrounding the limitations of the probing paradigm. In this work, we point out the inability to infer behavioral conclusions from probing results and offer an alternative method that focuses on how the information is being used, rather than on what information is encoded. Our method, Amnesic Probing, follows the intuition that the utility of a property for a given task can be assessed by measuring the influence of a causal intervention that removes it from the representation. Equipped with this new analysis tool, we can ask questions that were not possible before, e.g. is part-of-speech information important for word prediction? We perform a series of analyses on BERT to answer these types of questions. Our findings demonstrate that conventional probing performance is not correlated to task importance, and we call for increased scrutiny of claims that draw behavioral or causal conclusions from probing results.

papers.title: Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Networks for an Accurate and Interpretable Prediction of Material Properties
papers.research_question: How can we develop a machine learning framework that directly learns material properties from the atomic connection in a crystal, providing both accurate predictions and interpretable chemical insights?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (CGCNN) framework, which directly learns material properties from crystal graphs, achieving DFT-level accuracy for diverse properties and enabling the extraction of local chemical environment contributions for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The CGCNN framework provides a flexible, accurate, and interpretable method for predicting material properties and extracting design knowledge, as demonstrated by its application to perovskite discovery.
papers.key_findings:
CGCNN achieves prediction accuracy comparable to DFT calculations for eight different material properties using around 10^4 training data points.
The framework is interpretable, allowing extraction of site-specific energy contributions, as demonstrated for perovskite structures.
The learned site energy information can be used to derive empirical rules for material design, significantly reducing the search space for high-throughput screening.
A modified convolution function (Eq. 5) that differentiates interaction strengths between neighbors significantly improves prediction performance over a simpler version (Eq. 4).
CGCNN can predict both continuous properties (e.g., formation energy) and discrete properties (e.g., metal/semiconductor classification) with high accuracy.
papers.limitation: The initial convolution function (Eq. 4) uses a shared weight matrix for all neighbors of an atom, which neglects differences in interaction strength between neighbors.
papers.abstract: The use of machine learning methods for accelerating the design of crystalline materials usually requires manually constructed feature vectors or complex transformation of atom coordinates to input the crystal structure, which either constrains the model to certain crystal types or makes it difficult to provide chemical insights. Here, we develop a crystal graph convolutional neural networks framework to directly learn material properties from the connection of atoms in the crystal, providing a universal and interpretable representation of crystalline materials. Our method provides a highly accurate prediction of density functional theory calculated properties for eight different properties of crystals with various structure types and compositions after being trained with 10^{4} data points. Further, our framework is interpretable because one can extract the contributions from local chemical environments to global properties. Using an example of perovskites, we show how this information can be utilized to discover empirical rules for materials design.

papers.title: System-Mediated Attention Imbalances Make Vision-Language Models Say Yes
papers.research_question: Does system-mediated attention imbalance (redundant system attention leading to insufficient image and text attention) cause the yes-bias hallucination in vision-language models, as opposed to the image-centric hypothesis?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that system-mediated attention imbalances (redundant system attention causing insufficient image and text attention) are a key factor in the yes-bias hallucination in VLMs, and that redistributing attention from the system modality to image and text modalities effectively suppresses this bias.
papers.conclusion: System-mediated attention imbalances are a key driver of the yes-bias in VLMs, and redistributing system attention to image and text modalities is an effective mitigation strategy, highlighting the importance of a holistic view of attention allocation.
papers.key_findings:
Redistributing system attention to image and text modalities substantially suppresses the yes-bias, outperforming image-centric and text-suppressing methods.
The yes-bias is driven by redundant system attention in late decoder layers, which causes attention imbalances harming both image and text processing.
System-mediated attention imbalances encourage reliance on coarse input representations, which is detrimental for compositional tasks requiring fine-grained analysis.
The system-mediated hypothesis is empirically superior to the image-centric hypothesis for the yes-bias.
The effects of attention redistribution vary across tasks and model scales, with larger models showing less consistent gains.
papers.limitation:
Focus on LLaVA-based architectures and single-token generation in yes/no contexts, limiting generality.
Use of zero-ablation with complete redistribution prevents exploration of partial redistributions.
Interventions at the quarter level due to computational constraints, precluding per-layer analysis.
Representation-level mechanisms are inferred from performance and attention weights, not directly probed.
future_direction: Explore implications for autoregressive hallucination.
Apply holistic causal interventions to other manifestations of VLM hallucination.
Investigate redundant system attention in text-only LLMs.
papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) hallucination is commonly linked to imbalanced allocation of attention across input modalities: system, image and text. However, existing mitigation strategies tend towards an image-centric interpretation of these imbalances, often prioritising increased image attention while giving less consideration to the roles of the other modalities. In this study, we evaluate a more holistic, system-mediated account, which attributes these imbalances to functionally redundant system weights that reduce attention to image and textual inputs. We show that this framework offers a useful empirical perspective on the yes-bias, a common form of hallucination in which VLMs indiscriminately respond 'yes'. Causally redistributing attention from the system modality to image and textual inputs substantially suppresses this bias, often outperforming existing approaches. We further present evidence suggesting that system-mediated attention imbalances contribute to the yes-bias by encouraging a default reliance on coarse input representations, which are effective for some tasks but ill-suited to others. Taken together, these findings firmly establish system attention as a key factor in VLM hallucination and highlight its potential as a lever for mitigation.

papers.title: Improving Causal Interventions in Amnesic Probing with Mean Projection or LEACE
papers.research_question: Does using more precise information removal methods (Mean Projection and LEACE) instead of Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) improve the ability to uncover behavioral explanations via amnesic probing?
papers.core_contribution: Mean Projection (MP) and LEACE are more precise than Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) for removing target information in amnesic probing, causing less distortion to the representation space and leading to more reliable causal explanations of model behavior.
papers.conclusion: MP and LEACE outperform INLP in amnesic probing experiments, providing more precise information removal and thus more reliable causal explanations of model behavior; MP is recommended for its efficiency, with LEACE as a complementary method for verification.
papers.key_findings:
MP and LEACE remove target linguistic information more precisely than INLP while causing less distortion to the remaining representation space.
When using MP or LEACE, the performance drop on the main task (language modeling) is greater for target information removal than for removing a comparable amount of random information, which is not consistently the case with INLP.
Performance on the main task is restored more effectively when explicit gold labels of the target information are added back to the MP- or LEACE-modified space compared to the INLP-modified space.
MP and LEACE require far fewer projections than INLP to remove information, reducing computational cost and unintended side effects.
MP is sensitive to outliers in the data, which can affect the calculated projection directions.
papers.limitation:
MP is sensitive to outliers, as the mean of a class can be disproportionately influenced by extreme values, potentially misaligning the projection direction.
Reproduced results for INLP differ from the original study due to random factors in the INLP method (e.g., initialization, seeds), affecting the number of iterations needed.
The experiments are limited to three linguistic properties (dependency, f-pos, c-pos) and one model (BERT), so the findings may not generalize to other properties or models.
Results are based on a single run due to computational constraints, though tests indicated stability across runs.
papers.abstract: Amnesic probing is a technique used to examine the influence of specific linguistic information on the behaviour of a model.This involves identifying and removing the relevant information and then assessing whether the model's performance on the main task changes.If the removed information is relevant, the model's performance should decline.The difficulty with this approach lies in removing only the target information while leaving other information unchanged.It has been shown that Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP), a widely used removal technique, introduces random modifications to representations when eliminating target information.We demonstrate that Mean Projection (MP) and LEACE, two proposed alternatives, remove information in a more targeted manner, thereby enhancing the potential for obtaining behavioural explanations through Amnesic Probing.

papers.title: Factual Probing Is [MASK]: Learning vs. Learning to Recall
papers.research_question: Can we interpret factual probing results as a lower bound on the factual information encoded in a language model, or do prompt-search methods learn from the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OPTI PROMPT, a continuous prompt optimization method that improves factual probing accuracy, and shows that optimized prompts can exploit regularities in training data, complicating the interpretation of probing results.
papers.conclusion: OPTI PROMPT is an effective method for factual probing, but data-driven prompt optimization can exploit training data regularities, making it challenging to interpret probing results as a pure lower bound on model knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
OPTI PROMPT improves top-1 accuracy on the LAMA benchmark by 6.4% over previous methods.
Training data for factual probing contains regularities (e.g., class priors, lexical correlations) that can be exploited by prompt optimization methods.
Optimized prompts can predict facts even when probing randomly initialized models, indicating they learn from training data rather than solely eliciting stored knowledge.
Partitioning test facts into 'easy' (predictable from training data) and 'hard' subsets reveals that OPTI PROMPT improves on both, suggesting it is better at learning from data and eliciting facts from the language model.
Continuous prompt optimization is more efficient and effective than discrete token search, but requires white-box model access.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to determine whether a prediction comes from the language model's stored knowledge or from patterns learned from the training data during prompt optimization.
Gradient-based prompt optimization methods like OPTI PROMPT require white-box access to the model, limiting their use with API-based large models.
future_direction: Develop techniques for attributing predictions to specific training instances to better understand the source of factual knowledge.
Pursue more mechanistic explanations for how language models learn and represent factual information, beyond prompt-based probing.
papers.abstract: demonstrated that it is possible to retrieve world facts from a pretrained language model by expressing them as cloze-style prompts and interpret the model's prediction accuracy as a lower bound on the amount of factual information it encodes. Subsequent work has attempted to tighten the estimate by searching for better prompts, using a disjoint set of facts as training data. In this work, we make two complementary contributions to better understand these factual probing techniques. First, we propose OPTIPROMPT, a novel and efficient method which directly optimizes in continuous embedding space. We find this simple method is able to predict an additional 6.4% of facts in the LAMA benchmark. Second, we raise a more important question: Can we really interpret these probing results as a lower bound? Is it possible that these prompt-search methods learn from the training data too? We find, somewhat surprisingly, that the training data used by these methods contains certain regularities of the underlying fact distribution, and all the existing prompt methods, including ours, are able to exploit them for better fact prediction. We conduct a set of control experiments to disentangle "learning" from "learning to recall", providing a more detailed picture of what different prompts can reveal about pre-trained language models.

papers.title: Deep Supervised, but Not Unsupervised, Models May Explain IT Cortical Representation
papers.research_question: To what extent can the internal representations of computational object-vision models explain the representational geometry of primate inferior temporal (IT) cortex?
papers.core_contribution: Supervised deep learning models, particularly a deep convolutional network trained on ImageNet, best explain the representational geometry of primate IT cortex, and combining their features with linear discriminants can fully explain the IT data, whereas unsupervised models fail to account for the categorical clustering in IT.
papers.conclusion: Explaining IT cortical representation requires computational features trained through supervised learning with large labeled datasets to emphasize behaviorally important categorical divisions.
papers.key_findings:
Better performing models in object categorization show higher representational similarity to IT cortex.
Unsupervised models fail to explain the categorical clustering (e.g., animate/inanimate, face clusters) observed in IT.
A deep supervised convolutional network (trained on ImageNet) best explains IT representation but does not fully explain it.
Combining features from the deep supervised model with linear discriminants (trained to maximize categorical margins) yields a representation that fully explains the IT data.
Model representations that are more similar to IT also afford better categorization accuracy.
papers.abstract: Inferior temporal (IT) cortex in human and nonhuman primates serves visual object recognition. Computational object-vision models, although continually improving, do not yet reach human performance. It is unclear to what extent the internal representations of computational models can explain the IT representation. Here we investigate a wide range of computational model representations (37 in total), testing their categorization performance and their ability to account for the IT representational geometry. The models include well-known neuroscientific object-recognition models (e.g. HMAX, VisNet) along with several models from computer vision (e.g. SIFT, GIST, self-similarity features, and a deep convolutional neural network). We compared the representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) of the model representations with the RDMs obtained from human IT (measured with fMRI) and monkey IT (measured with cell recording) for the same set of stimuli (not used in training the models). Better performing models were more similar to IT in that they showed greater clustering of representational patterns by category. In addition, better performing models also more strongly resembled IT in terms of their within-category representational dissimilarities. Representational geometries were significantly correlated between IT and many of the models. However, the categorical clustering observed in IT was largely unexplained by the unsupervised models. The deep convolutional network, which was trained by supervision with over a million category-labeled images, reached the highest categorization performance and also best explained IT, although it did not fully explain the IT data. Combining the features of this model with appropriate weights and adding linear combinations that maximize the margin between animate and inanimate objects and between faces and other objects yielded a representation that fully explained our IT data. Overall, our results suggest that explaining IT requires computational features trained through supervised learning to emphasize the behaviorally important categorical divisions prominently reflected in IT.

papers.title: InfoGAN: Interpretable Representation Learning by Information Maximizing Generative Adversarial Nets
papers.research_question: How can we learn interpretable and disentangled representations from data in a completely unsupervised manner?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces InfoGAN, an information-theoretic extension to GANs that learns disentangled representations by maximizing mutual information between a subset of latent variables and the observation, without requiring any supervision.
papers.conclusion: InfoGAN is a completely unsupervised method that learns interpretable and disentangled representations on complex datasets with negligible extra computation cost and is easy to train.
papers.key_findings:
InfoGAN successfully maximizes mutual information, as shown by the variational lower bound LI quickly reaching the entropy of the latent codes.
On MNIST, InfoGAN disentangles digit shape (categorical code) from style variations like rotation and width (continuous codes).
On 3D face and chair datasets, InfoGAN discovers latent factors corresponding to azimuth, elevation, lighting, and object width without supervision.
On SVHN, InfoGAN separates lighting variation and the context of the central digit from the digit itself.
On CelebA, InfoGAN learns to represent high-level semantic concepts like pose, presence of eyeglasses, hairstyle, and emotion.
future_direction: Applying the mutual information maximization idea to other generative models like VAEs.
Learning hierarchical latent representations.
Improving semi-supervised learning with better latent codes.
Using InfoGAN as a high-dimensional data discovery tool.
papers.abstract: This paper describes InfoGAN, an information-theoretic extension to the Generative Adversarial Network that is able to learn disentangled representations in a completely unsupervised manner. InfoGAN is a generative adversarial network that also maximizes the mutual information between a small subset of the latent variables and the observation. We derive a lower bound to the mutual information objective that can be optimized efficiently, and show that our training procedure can be interpreted as a variation of the Wake-Sleep algorithm. Specifically, InfoGAN successfully disentangles writing styles from digit shapes on the MNIST dataset, pose from lighting of 3D rendered images, and background digits from the central digit on the SVHN dataset. It also discovers visual concepts that include hair styles, presence/absence of eyeglasses, and emotions on the CelebA face dataset. Experiments show that InfoGAN learns interpretable representations that are competitive with representations learned by existing fully supervised methods.

papers.title: Visualizing and Understanding Recurrent Networks
papers.research_question: How do LSTMs and other recurrent networks learn and represent long-range dependencies in sequential data, and what are the sources of their limitations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides an empirical analysis of LSTM and GRU models on character-level language modeling, revealing interpretable cells that track long-range dependencies and quantifying the source of their performance gains and remaining errors through comparison with finite-context models.
papers.conclusion: LSTMs learn powerful and often interpretable long-range interactions on real-world data, but error analysis suggests that simply scaling the model may not address all limitations, pointing to a need for new architectural innovations.
papers.key_findings:
LSTMs develop interpretable memory cells that track long-range structural dependencies like line lengths, quotes, and brackets.
LSTMs significantly outperform finite-context n-gram models on characters requiring long-range reasoning, such as closing braces and carriage returns.
Error analysis reveals that scaling model size primarily reduces errors related to short-range (n-gram) dependencies, leaving other error categories largely unchanged.
Training dynamics show that LSTMs gradually learn to model dependencies over increasing time horizons.
Gate activation statistics show distinct saturation patterns across network layers, with first-layer gates operating in a more diffuse regime.
papers.limitation: The error analysis is dependent on the order in which oracles are applied.
future_direction: Using dynamic evaluation or memory networks to address the dynamic memory limitation.
Using unsupervised pretraining or more data to address rare word errors.
Exploring hierarchical context models to improve word-level predictions.
papers.abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and specifically a variant with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), are enjoying renewed interest as a result of successful applications in a wide range of machine learning problems that involve sequential data. However, while LSTMs provide exceptional results in practice, the source of their performance and their limitations remain rather poorly understood. Using character-level language models as an interpretable testbed, we aim to bridge this gap by providing an analysis of their representations, predictions and error types. In particular, our experiments reveal the existence of interpretable cells that keep track of long-range dependencies such as line lengths, quotes and brackets. Moreover, our comparative analysis with finite horizon n-gram models traces the source of the LSTM improvements to long-range structural dependencies. Finally, we provide analysis of the remaining errors and suggests areas for further study.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
