papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Analyzing Multi-Head Self-Attention: Specialized Heads Do the Heavy Lifting, the Rest Can Be Pruned
papers.research_question: To what extent does translation quality depend on individual encoder heads? Do individual encoder heads play consistent and interpretable roles? Which types of model attention are most sensitive to the number of heads? Can we significantly reduce the number of attention heads while preserving translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that only a small subset of attention heads in the Transformer are important for translation, and these heads perform interpretable functions (positional, syntactic, rare words). It introduces a pruning method based on stochastic gates and L0 penalty relaxation that can remove the majority of heads with minimal performance drop.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that only a small subset of attention heads are important for translation, and these heads perform interpretable functions. The proposed pruning method demonstrates that the vast majority of heads, especially encoder self-attention heads, can be removed without significant performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small subset of attention heads are important for translation.
Important heads have specialized and interpretable functions, such as attending to adjacent tokens (positional), tracking specific syntactic dependencies, or attending to rare words.
The proposed pruning method can remove the vast majority of heads without seriously affecting performance (e.g., pruning 38 out of 48 encoder heads results in only 0.15 BLEU drop on WMT EN-RU).
Specialized heads (positional and syntactic) are the last to be pruned, confirming their importance.
Encoder self-attention heads are pruned first, while decoder-encoder attention heads are the most important for translation.
future_direction: Investigate how the pruning method compares to alternative methods of model compression in neural machine translation.
papers.abstract: Multi-head self-attention is a key component of the Transformer, a state-of-the-art architecture for neural machine translation. In this work we evaluate the contribution made by individual attention heads in the encoder to the overall performance of the model and analyze the roles played by them. We find that the most important and confident heads play consistent and often linguistically-interpretable roles. When pruning heads using a method based on stochastic gates and a differentiable relaxation of the L 0 penalty, we observe that specialized heads are last to be pruned. Our novel pruning method removes the vast majority of heads without seriously affecting performance. For example, on the English-Russian WMT dataset, pruning 38 out of 48 encoder heads results in a drop of only 0.15 BLEU. 1

papers.title: If Attention Serves as a Cognitive Model of Human Memory Retrieval, What is the Plausible Memory Representation?
papers.research_question: Investigates whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Transformer Grammar's attention, operating on syntactic structures, better predicts human reading times than vanilla Transformer, suggesting dual memory representations in human sentence processing with attention as a general memory retrieval algorithm.
papers.conclusion: Attention can serve as the general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from two representational systems, and Transformer Grammar, with its syntactic structure-based attention, best captures dominant factors in human sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
TG's NAE has stronger predictive power for reading times than Transformer's NAE.
TG's and Transformer's NAE have independent contributions to reading time prediction, suggesting they capture distinct aspects of memory retrieval.
TG's NAE captures interference effects, independent of decay effects modeled by Category Locality Theory.
TG's advantage over TG−comp indicates the importance of treating closed phrases as single representations (via COMPOSE attention) for capturing syntax-based memory retrieval.
The attention mechanism serves as a general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from dual representational systems (syntactic and token-based).
papers.limitation:
The NAE calculation procedure (summing across heads, handling subwords) strictly followed Oh and Schuler (2022), but alternative approaches warrant investigation.
The findings are based on the English Natural Stories corpus; generalizability to other languages and cognitive measures (e.g., gaze duration, EEG) remains to be investigated.
The use of 'perfect oracles' for syntactic structures idealizes away from local ambiguities that humans encounter during actual sentence processing.
future_direction: Incorporate more realistic elements such as parallel parsing, left-corner parsing strategies, and memory decay mechanisms to fully operate at the algorithmic level.
Investigate generalizability to different languages and other measures of cognitive load.
Explore alternative approaches to handling layers, attention heads, and subword tokens in NAE calculation.
papers.abstract: Recent work in computational psycholinguistics has revealed intriguing parallels between attention mechanisms and human memory retrieval, focusing primarily on vanilla Transformers that operate on token-level representations. However, computational psycholinguistic research has also established that syntactic structures provide compelling explanations for human sentence processing that token-level factors cannot fully account for. In this paper, we investigate whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis between models and humans. Our experiments demonstrate that TG's attention achieves superior predictive power for self-paced reading times compared to vanilla Transformer's, with further analyses revealing independent contributions from both models. These findings suggest that human sentence processing involves dual memory representations -- one based on syntactic structures and another on token sequences -- with attention serving as the general memory retrieval algorithm, while highlighting the importance of incorporating syntactic structures as representational units.

papers.title: Memorization Without Overfitting: Analyzing the Training Dynamics of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do memorization and forgetting dynamics in language models change during training, and how do they depend on factors like model size, dataset size, and learning rate?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models memorize training data faster and forget less throughout training, with nouns and numbers being memorized more quickly than other parts of speech.
papers.conclusion: Memorization dynamics are a critical metric for understanding language model training, with larger models exhibiting faster memorization and less forgetting, highlighting the importance of analyzing memorization alongside cross-entropy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Larger language models memorize training data faster across various settings (causal and masked LM, different dataset sizes).
Larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before overfitting occurs.
Forgetting curves approach a baseline (the forgetting baseline), and this baseline increases with model scale, meaning larger models forget less.
Nouns and numbers are memorized much faster than other parts of speech, acting as unique identifiers for training examples.
Adding unique identifiers (like document IDs) to training examples increases memorization speed.
papers.limitation:
The exact memorization metric (Definition 1) ignores model confidence and does not normalize for duplication in the training set.
The focus on exact memorization may not capture all aspects of privacy, as it only considers verbatim output of sensitive information.
future_direction: Understanding the structure of the forgetting baseline, e.g., what types of tokens (parts of speech, synonyms, facts) are memorized in the baseline.
Analyzing memorization dynamics as a critical metric when scaling up language models, beyond just cross-entropy loss.
papers.abstract: Despite their wide adoption, the underlying training and memorization dynamics of very large language models is not well understood. We empirically study exact memorization in causal and masked language modeling, across model sizes and throughout the training process. We measure the effects of dataset size, learning rate, and model size on memorization, finding that larger language models memorize training data faster across all settings. Surprisingly, we show that larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before over-fitting and tend to forget less throughout the training process. We also analyze the memorization dynamics of different parts of speech and find that models memorize nouns and numbers first; we hypothesize and provide empirical evidence that nouns and numbers act as a unique identifier for memorizing individual training examples. Together, these findings present another piece of the broader puzzle of trying to understand what actually improves as models get bigger.

papers.title: Aspects of human memory and Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do Large Language Models exhibit human-like memory properties such as primacy and recency effects, and are these properties due to architectural biases or learned from training data?
papers.core_contribution: Large Language Models exhibit human-like memory properties such as primacy and recency effects, and these properties are likely learned from the statistical patterns in training data rather than being inherent to the transformer architecture.
papers.conclusion: The human-like memory properties observed in Large Language Models are likely learned from statistical patterns in human-generated text, suggesting that human memory characteristics influence the structure of narratives.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit primacy and recency effects in memory recall.
Adding elaborations to facts improves recall accuracy.
Forgetting in LLMs occurs primarily through interference rather than memory decay.
Repetitions improve recall, with spaced repetitions being more effective than immediate ones.
LLMs show a 'memory formation time' where recall improves with initial distance from the presented facts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are huge artificial neural networks which primarily serve to generate text, but also provide a very sophisticated probabilistic model of language use. Since generating a semantically consistent text requires a form of effective memory, we investigate the memory properties of LLMs and find surprising similarities with key characteristics of human memory. We argue that the human-like memory properties of the Large Language Model do not follow automatically from the LLM architecture but are rather learned from the statistics of the training textual data. These results strongly suggest that the biological features of human memory leave an imprint on the way that we structure our textual narratives.

papers.title: DeCoRe: Decoding by Contrasting Retrieval Heads to Mitigate Hallucinations
papers.research_question: Can masking retrieval heads induce hallucinations, and can contrasting the outputs of the base LLM and the masked LLM reduce hallucinations, specifically improving contextual faithfulness, factual recall, and multi-hop reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DeCoRe, a training-free decoding strategy that contrasts base and masked LLM outputs to mitigate hallucinations, using conditional entropy to dynamically control the contrast.
papers.conclusion: DeCoRe effectively mitigates hallucinations by contrasting base and masked LLM outputs, improving faithfulness, factuality, and reasoning across multiple tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
DeCoRe significantly improves contextual faithfulness on summarization (XSum), instruction following (MemoTrap), and open-book QA (NQ-Open, NQ-Swap).
DeCoRe improves factual recall on TriviaQA, PopQA, and TruthfulQA, indicating it mitigates factuality hallucinations.
DeCoRe enhances multi-hop reasoning when combined with Chain-of-Thought prompting, as shown on MuSiQue.
Masking retrieval heads induces hallucinations, validating their role in information retrieval.
Dynamic entropy-controlled contrastive decoding (DeCoRe_entropy) outperforms static versions and baselines in many tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often hallucinate, producing unfaithful or factually incorrect outputs by misrepresenting the provided context or incorrectly recalling internal knowledge. Recent studies have identified specific attention heads within the Transformer architecture, known as retrieval heads, responsible for extracting relevant contextual information. We hypothesise that masking these retrieval heads can induce hallucinations and that contrasting the outputs of the base LLM and the masked LLM can reduce hallucinations. To this end, we propose Decoding by Contrasting Retrieval Heads (DeCoRe), a novel training-free decoding strategy that amplifies information found in the context and model parameters. DeCoRe mitigates potentially hallucinated responses by dynamically contrasting the outputs of the base LLM and the masked LLM, using conditional entropy as a guide. Our extensive experiments confirm that DeCoRe significantly improves performance on tasks requiring high contextual faithfulness, such as summarisation (XSum by 18.6%), instruction following (MemoTrap by 10.9%), and open-book question answering (NQ-Open by 2.4% and NQ-Swap by 5.5%).

papers.title: Opening the Black Box of Deep Neural Networks via Information
papers.research_question: How do deep neural networks organize information during training, and do they optimize the Information Bottleneck tradeoff between compression and prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that DNN training has two distinct phases: empirical error minimization and representation compression, and that the converged layers lie on or very close to the Information Bottleneck theoretical bound.
papers.conclusion: Deep Learning with DNNs are in essence learning algorithms that effectively find efficient representations that are approximate minimal sufficient statistics in the Information Bottleneck sense.
papers.key_findings:
Stochastic Gradient Descent optimization has two phases: a drift phase (empirical error minimization) and a diffusion phase (representation compression).
The converged layers of DNNs lie on or very close to the Information Bottleneck bound, satisfying the self-consistent equations.
Adding hidden layers dramatically reduces the number of training epochs required for good generalization, indicating a computational benefit.
The compression phase is responsible for the absence of overfitting in deep learning.
The hidden layers appear to converge to critical points on the Information Bottleneck curve.
papers.limitation: The findings need to be verified on larger networks, other architectures, and real-world problems.
future_direction: Developing new learning algorithms that utilize the claimed IB optimality of the layers.
Combining IB iterations with stochastic relaxation methods to boost DNN training.
papers.abstract: Despite their great success, there is still no comprehensive theoretical understanding of learning with Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) or their inner organization. Previous work proposed to analyze DNNs in the \textit{Information Plane}; i.e., the plane of the Mutual Information values that each layer preserves on the input and output variables. They suggested that the goal of the network is to optimize the Information Bottleneck (IB) tradeoff between compression and prediction, successively, for each layer. In this work we follow up on this idea and demonstrate the effectiveness of the Information-Plane visualization of DNNs. Our main results are: (i) most of the training epochs in standard DL are spent on {\emph compression} of the input to efficient representation and not on fitting the training labels. (ii) The representation compression phase begins when the training errors becomes small and the Stochastic Gradient Decent (SGD) epochs change from a fast drift to smaller training error into a stochastic relaxation, or random diffusion, constrained by the training error value. (iii) The converged layers lie on or very close to the Information Bottleneck (IB) theoretical bound, and the maps from the input to any hidden layer and from this hidden layer to the output satisfy the IB self-consistent equations. This generalization through noise mechanism is unique to Deep Neural Networks and absent in one layer networks. (iv) The training time is dramatically reduced when adding more hidden layers. Thus the main advantage of the hidden layers is computational. This can be explained by the reduced relaxation time, as this it scales super-linearly (exponentially for simple diffusion) with the information compression from the previous layer.

papers.title: Uncovering Grounding IDs: How External Cues Shape Multimodal Binding
papers.research_question: Why do external cues improve reasoning in large vision-language models (LVLMs)? The paper investigates how external visual and textual cues induce latent identifiers (Grounding IDs) that improve cross-modal alignment and reduce hallucinations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that external visual and textual cues induce latent identifiers (Grounding IDs) in LVLMs, which enhance cross-modal alignment, reduce hallucinations, and improve visual reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Grounding IDs are a key mechanism for partition-based binding, providing mechanistic insight into how external cues improve multimodal grounding and reasoning in LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
External cues (symbols, grid lines) improve attention within partitions and cross-modal alignment.
Grounding IDs emerge as latent vectors that bind visual and textual tokens belonging to the same partition.
Activation swapping experiments show that object-symbol bindings are mediated by Grounding IDs, not local features.
Grounding IDs reduce the modality gap between visual and textual representations.
Structured inputs reduce hallucinations in long caption generation and improve performance on visual reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation: Structured inputs may have lower recall in object presence questions due to objects spanning grid boundaries or being positioned across partitions.
future_direction: Discovering circuits that support system-2 reasoning tasks, such as counting and spatial reasoning.
Integrating external cues during RL finetuning to strengthen the model's internal ability to perform sequential scanning based on provided cues.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) show strong performance across multimodal benchmarks but remain limited in structured reasoning and precise grounding. Recent work has demonstrated that adding simple visual structures, such as partitions and annotations, improves accuracy, yet the internal mechanisms underlying these gains remain unclear. We investigate this phenomenon and propose the concept of Grounding IDs, latent identifiers induced by external cues that bind objects to their designated partitions across modalities. Through representation analysis, we find that these identifiers emerge as consistent within-partition alignment in embedding space and reduce the modality gap between image and text. Causal interventions further confirm that these identifiers mediate binding between objects and symbolic cues. We show that Grounding IDs strengthen attention between related components, which in turn improves cross-modal grounding and reduces hallucinations. Taken together, our results identify Grounding IDs as a key symbolic mechanism that explains how external cues enhance multimodal binding and offer both interpretability and practical improvements.

papers.title: Dynamic Memory Inference Network for Natural Language Inference (2017)
papers.research_question: How can Dynamic Memory Networks be applied to improve performance in Natural Language Inference tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Dynamic Memory Networks are effective for Natural Language Inference by leveraging episodic memory updates and attention mechanisms, improving inference accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The Dynamic Memory Network framework effectively enhances Natural Language Inference by integrating episodic memory updates and attention mechanisms, offering a promising approach for future NLP tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Dynamic Memory Networks with episodic memory updates improve accuracy in Natural Language Inference tasks.
Attention mechanisms in DMNs enable the model to focus on critical parts of sentences for better inference.
Multi-hop reasoning allows the model to revisit and refine memory states, mimicking human cognitive processes.
The proposed approach shows potential for complex NLI tasks but has computational limitations.
Experiments on SNLI dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of DMNs over traditional encoding methods.
papers.limitation: Training DMNs is time-consuming and computationally expensive due to multiple memory hops and attention mechanisms.
future_direction: Reducing computational complexity and optimizing memory structures in DMNs.
Integrating advanced sentence encoders like transformers to capture long-distance dependencies.
Extending DMN framework to other NLP domains such as dialogue systems and question answering.
papers.abstract: In this paper, the NLI task is viewed as a question - and - answer problem, which leads to proposing the application of DMNs to enhance performance. NLI classifies the relationship between two sentences as entailment, contradiction, or neutral. It is necessary for many NLP applications, including question - answering, text summarization, and information retrieval. The most significant contribution of the paper is to demonstrate that DMNs are effective for episodic memory and experiment with DMNs outside of their original domain. This feature allows the model to incrementally update and reawaken memory, which provides a more nuanced view of the interactions of the sentences and hence also improves the accuracy of its inferential process. Furthermore, the paper analyses the aspects of the employed attention mechanisms in the structure of DMNs that enhance the capability of the model to pay attention to the essential words and phrases for successful task completion. The study highlights the impact of integrating the episodic memory updates with the attention mechanisms due to extensive experimentation, showing the benefits of such an NLI improvement and the potential for enhancing other NLP tasks.

papers.title: Object Detectors Emerge in Deep Scene CNNs
papers.research_question: What is the nature of the representation learned by a CNN trained for scene classification, and does object detection emerge as part of this representation?
papers.core_contribution: Object detectors emerge in the inner layers of a CNN trained for scene classification, enabling the same network to perform both scene recognition and object localization in a single forward pass without explicit object-level supervision.
papers.conclusion: A single network can support recognition at multiple levels of abstraction (edges, textures, objects, scenes) without needing multiple outputs or networks, as object detectors emerge naturally when training for scene classification.
papers.key_findings:
A CNN trained on scene classification (Places) learns object detectors in its inner layers, even more so than a CNN trained on object classification (ImageNet).
The network learns a hierarchy of features, with early layers responding to simple elements and textures, and later layers responding to objects and scenes.
The objects that emerge are the most discriminative for the scene classification task, as evidenced by a high correlation between object frequency in the network and object informativeness for scene classification.
The network can perform object localization using the activations of its internal units, with high segmentation performance for many object classes.
Not all units in the network are object detectors; some may encode textures or other scene features, indicating a complementary representation.
papers.limitation: Only objects that are informative for the specific scene recognition task emerge; other object classes may not be learned.
future_direction: Explore which other tasks would allow for other object classes to be learned without explicit object-level supervision.
papers.abstract: With the success of new computational architectures for visual processing, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN) and access to image databases with millions of labeled examples (e.g., ImageNet, Places), the state of the art in computer vision is advancing rapidly. One important factor for continued progress is to understand the representations that are learned by the inner layers of these deep architectures. Here we show that object detectors emerge from training CNNs to perform scene classification. As scenes are composed of objects, the CNN for scene classification automatically discovers meaningful objects detectors, representative of the learned scene categories. With object detectors emerging as a result of learning to recognize scenes, our work demonstrates that the same network can perform both scene recognition and object localization in a single forward-pass, without ever having been explicitly taught the notion of objects.

papers.title: Dissecting Lottery Ticket Transformers: Structural and Behavioral Study\n of Sparse Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does iterative magnitude pruning affect the learned representations and internal components of Transformers for neural machine translation, and what are the differences in behavior between sparse and dense models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that iterative magnitude pruning degrades complex semantic knowledge first, causes higher layers to diverge and become less complex, shifts encoding burden to early layers, and leaves attention mechanisms largely unchanged.
papers.conclusion: The paper evaluates how unstructured pruning affects Transformer behavior while task performance is maintained, showing pruning degrades semantic knowledge before BLEU, early sparse layers better encode low-level information, representational changes occur especially in higher layers, and attention distributions remain similar.
papers.key_findings:
Complex semantic information is lost first during pruning, before BLEU decreases.
Model activations steadily diverge from unpruned representations, particularly at higher layers.
Information flow becomes more distributed in sparse Transformers: lower layers perform more encoding.
Attention mechanisms remain remarkably consistent across sparsities.
Encoder-decoder attention is the richest in representation, whereas decoder self-attention is the simplest.
papers.limitation:
BLEU is an imperfect measure of translation quality, so pruned models might perform worse than suggested.
The work focuses solely on magnitude pruning, which may not be representative of other pruning methods.
Probing classifiers measure correlation between model outputs and auxiliary information, not necessarily what information the model uses during its forward pass.
future_direction: Future work could analyze a model's encoded knowledge in other ways beyond probing.
Differences in how directly sparse and dense models encode information could be studied using minimum description lengths.
papers.abstract:
Recent work on the lottery ticket hypothesis has produced highly sparse
Transformers for NMT while maintaining BLEU. However, it is unclear how such
pruning techniques affect a model's learned representations. By probing
Transformers with more and more low-magnitude weights pruned away, we find that
complex semantic information is first to be degraded. Analysis of internal
activations reveals that higher layers diverge most over the course of pruning,
gradually becoming less complex than their dense counterparts. Meanwhile, early
layers of sparse models begin to perform more encoding. Attention mechanisms
remain remarkably consistent as sparsity increases.

papers.title: Abstraction in time: Finding hierarchical linguistic structure in a model of relational processing
papers.research_question: Does the oscillatory activation in LISA/DORA models during processing match human cortical activity during language processing, suggesting a common mechanism for hierarchical representation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LISA/DORA models of relational processing exhibit oscillatory activation patterns during sentence processing that closely match human cortical tracking of hierarchical linguistic structures, suggesting that mechanisms for relational binding may underlie language representation.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that abstract hierarchical linguistic representations can be processed by models of relational reasoning, and suggests that integrating such models with language processing models could advance cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
LISA/DORA models parse English sentences and show firing patterns that mirror cortical activity observed in Ding et al. (2016), with activation bursts at sentence (1Hz), phrasal (2Hz), and syllabic (4Hz) rates.
The models' binding mechanisms, using temporal synchrony and asynchrony, naturally produce hierarchical representations similar to those in human language processing.
These models, built for analogy and relational learning, generalize to language processing without modification, unlike grammar-based or statistical models.
The results support the idea that relational role representation may be a foundation for human cognitive capacities like language.
Integrating models of relational reasoning and language processing could lead to more plausible cognitive models.
future_direction: Testing on natural speech input
Testing on varied syntactic structures
Testing in rich discourse contexts and multilingual input
papers.abstract: Abstract mental representation is fundamental for human cognition. Forming such representations in time, especially from dynamic and noisy perceptual input, is a challenge for any processing modality, but perhaps none so acutely as for language processing. We show that LISA (Hummel & Holyaok, 1997) and DORA (Doumas, Hummel, & Sandhofer, 2008), models built to process and to learn structured (i.e., symbolic) rep resentations of conceptual properties and relations from unstructured inputs, show oscillatory activation during processing that is highly similar to the cortical activity elicited by the linguistic stimuli from Ding et al.(2016). We argue, as Ding et al.(2016), that this activation reflects formation of hierarchical linguistic representation, and furthermore, that the kind of computational mechanisms in LISA/DORA (e.g., temporal binding by systematic asynchrony of firing) may underlie formation of abstract linguistic representations in the human brain. It may be this repurposing that allowed for the generation or mergence of hierarchical linguistic structure, and therefore, human language, from extant cognitive and neural systems. We conclude that models of thinking and reasoning and models of language processing must be integrated —not only for increased plausiblity, but in order to advance both fields towards a larger integrative model of human cognition

papers.title: P-Tuning: Prompt Tuning Can Be Comparable to Fine-tuning Across Scales and Tasks
papers.research_question: Can prompt tuning be made comparable to fine-tuning across a wide range of model scales and NLU tasks?
papers.core_contribution: P-tuning v2, an optimized implementation of deep prompt tuning, matches fine-tuning performance across model scales (300M to 10B parameters) and NLU tasks while using only 0.1%-3% of task-specific parameters.
papers.conclusion: P-tuning v2 demonstrates that properly optimized prompt tuning can be a parameter-efficient alternative to fine-tuning and serves as a strong baseline for future research.
papers.key_findings:
P-tuning v2 matches fine-tuning performance across model scales from 300M to 10B parameters.
P-tuning v2 works effectively on both simple classification and hard sequence labeling tasks.
Multi-task learning can provide a better initialization and further boost performance.
Using a randomly-initialized linear classification head works as well as a verbalizer with LM head in a full-data setting.
Adding continuous prompts to deeper transformer layers (closer to the output) is more effective than adding them only at the input layer.
papers.limitation: The usefulness of reparameterization (e.g., using an MLP) depends on the task and dataset, sometimes leading to minimal or negative effects.
papers.abstract: Prompt tuning, which only tunes continuous prompts with a frozen language model, substantially reduces per-task storage and memory usage at training. However, in the context of NLU, prior work reveals that prompt tuning does not perform well for normal-sized pretrained models. We also find that existing methods of prompt tuning cannot handle hard sequence labeling tasks, indicating a lack of universality. We present a novel empirical finding that properly optimized prompt tuning can be universally effective across a wide range of model scales and NLU tasks. It matches the performance of finetuning while having only 0.1%-3% tuned parameters. Our method P-Tuning v2 is an implementation of Deep Prompt Tuning Given the universality and simplicity of P-Tuning v2, we believe it can serve as an alternative to finetuning and a strong baseline for future research. 1

papers.title: Language Modeling with Deep Transformers
papers.research_question: How to configure Transformer models for language modeling in speech recognition, and whether positional encoding is necessary for deep autoregressive Transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: Deep Transformer language models outperform LSTM-RNN baselines for speech recognition, and positional encoding is not required for autoregressive Transformers as they can inherently use positional information from the sequence.
papers.conclusion: Deep Transformer language models are effective for speech recognition and do not require positional encoding in the autoregressive setting, as the model can inherently use positional information from the increasing amount of information along the sequence.
papers.key_findings:
Deep Transformer language models outperform LSTM-RNN baselines on both word-level and BPE-level language modeling for speech recognition.
Removing positional encoding slightly improves performance in deep autoregressive Transformer language models.
The first layer of the Transformer with positional encoding learns to create n-gram features, while without positional encoding it focuses on the new input token.
Other layers in the Transformer exhibit three categories: 'blur' layers, 'window' layers, and 'structured' layers.
Parameter sharing across layers (Universal Transformers) does not perform as well as standard Transformers but shows improvement with more layers.
papers.limitation:
No regularization is applied, and scaling up model size and using regularization might improve performance further.
Universal Transformers require different hyperparameters (e.g., reduced gradient norm clipping) and converge slower.
future_direction: Apply Transformer components (e.g., layer normalization) to deeper LSTM models.
Scale up model size and use regularization to improve performance further.
papers.abstract: We explore deep autoregressive Transformer models in language modeling for speech recognition. We focus on two aspects. First, we revisit Transformer model configurations specifically for language modeling. We show that well configured Transformer models outperform our baseline models based on the shallow stack of LSTM recurrent neural network layers. We carry out experiments on the open-source LibriSpeech 960hr task, for both 200K vocabulary word-level and 10K byte-pair encoding subword-level language modeling. We apply our word-level models to conventional hybrid speech recognition by lattice rescoring, and the subword-level models to attention based encoder-decoder models by shallow fusion. Second, we show that deep Transformer language models do not require positional encoding. The positional encoding is an essential augmentation for the self-attention mechanism which is invariant to sequence ordering. However, in autoregressive setup, as is the case for language modeling, the amount of information increases along the position dimension, which is a positional signal by its own. The analysis of attention weights shows that deep autoregressive self-attention models can automatically make use of such positional information. We find that removing the positional encoding even slightly improves the performance of these models.

papers.title: Understanding deep convolutional networks
papers.research_question: What principles govern the properties of deep convolutional networks, specifically how they compute invariants through multiscale contractions, linearization of hierarchical symmetries, and sparse separations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework to analyze deep convolutional networks, showing that computations of invariants involve multiscale contractions, linearization of hierarchical symmetries, and sparse separations.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a mathematical framework for analyzing contraction and separation properties of deep convolutional networks, but further work is needed on complexity measures, approximation theorems, and optimization convergence.
papers.key_findings:
Deep convolutional networks compute invariants through multiscale contractions.
They linearize hierarchical symmetries to preserve separation.
Sparse separations are important for maintaining the classification margin.
The scattering transform provides invariance to translations and small deformations.
Network architecture can be understood through groups of symmetries and fiber bundles.
future_direction: Develop complexity measures for deep convolutional networks.
Establish approximation theorems in spaces of high-dimensional functions.
Prove guaranteed convergence of filter optimization algorithms.
papers.abstract: Deep convolutional networks provide state-of-the-art classifications and regressions results over many high-dimensional problems. We review their architecture, which scatters data with a cascade of linear filter weights and nonlinearities. A mathematical framework is introduced to analyse their properties. Computations of invariants involve multiscale contractions with wavelets, the linearization of hierarchical symmetries and sparse separations. Applications are discussed.

papers.title: When are Lemons Purple? The Concept Association Bias of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do vision-language models like CLIP struggle with tasks requiring fine-grained correspondence between vision and language, such as Visual Question Answering (VQA)? The paper investigates the Concept Association Bias (CAB) as a potential cause.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the Concept Association Bias (CAB) in vision-language models, showing that it is prevalent in contrastively trained models and that deeper cross-modal interaction through fine-tuning can mitigate it.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Association Bias (CAB) exists in vision-language models, particularly those trained with contrastive losses, and reducing CAB can improve performance on tasks like VQA, highlighting a brittleness in contrastive objectives.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP and other vision-language models exhibit Concept Association Bias (CAB), where they treat input as a bag of concepts and fill in missing concepts crossmodally, leading to errors in tasks like color recognition.
CAB is especially prominent in models trained with contrastive losses (e.g., CLIP, BLIP-contrast), while models trained solely with autoregressive loss (e.g., OFA) show minimal or no CAB.
The strength of CAB predicts performance on VQA-v2: models with lower CAB scores achieve higher accuracy on VQA.
Adding a Transformer head for deeper modality interaction and fine-tuning on VQA reduces CAB and improves VQA performance.
Fine-tuning may not fundamentally solve the binding problem, as models still struggle with unnatural color-object pairs, suggesting that fine-tuning simply allows models to pick up real-world co-occurrences.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to color and part-whole attributes, and does not explore other object-attribute relationships such as material, shape, or texture.
future_direction: Explore the effect of CAB on other vision-language tasks beyond VQA, such as visual entailment.
Investigate other object-attribute relationships beyond color and part-whole.
Study other vision-language models that incorporate more extensive modality interactions (e.g., FLAVA, ALBEF).
papers.abstract: Large-scale vision-language models such as CLIP have shown impressive performance on zero-shot image classification and image-to-text retrieval. However, such performance does not realize in tasks that require a finer-grained correspondence between vision and language, such as Visual Question Answering (VQA). We investigate why this is the case, and report an interesting phenomenon of vision-language models, which we call the Concept Association Bias (CAB), as a potential cause of the difficulty of applying these models to VQA and similar tasks. We find that models with CAB tend to treat input as a bag of concepts and attempt to fill in the other missing concept crossmodally, leading to an unexpected zero-shot prediction. We demonstrate CAB by showing that CLIP’s zero-shot classification performance greatly suffers when there is a strong concept association between an object (e.g. eggplant) and an attribute (e.g. color purple). We also show that the strength of CAB predicts the performance on VQA. We observe that CAB is prevalent in vision-language models trained with contrastive losses, even when autoregressive losses are jointly employed. However, a model that solely relies on autoregressive loss seems to exhibit minimal or no signs of CAB.

papers.title: What you can cram into a single $&!#* vector: Probing sentence embeddings for linguistic properties
papers.research_question: What linguistic properties are captured by sentence embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a set of 10 probing tasks to analyze the linguistic properties captured by sentence embeddings, and uses them to study embeddings from three different encoders trained in eight distinct ways.
papers.conclusion: The introduced probing tasks are a useful tool for understanding what linguistic information is captured by sentence embeddings, and the study reveals that modern encoders capture a wide range of linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Bag-of-Vectors (BoV) is surprisingly good at capturing sentence-level properties due to redundancies in natural language.
Different encoder architectures (BiLSTM, Gated ConvNet) lead to embeddings with different linguistic properties even when trained on the same objective.
BiLSTM-max embeddings capture interesting linguistic knowledge even without any training.
There are significant correlations between performance on probing tasks (especially Word Content) and downstream tasks.
Training on NMT leads to encoders more linguistically aware than those trained on NLI for the probing tasks, despite NLI being better for downstream tasks.
future_direction: Extend the probing tasks to other languages.
Investigate how multi-task training affects probing task performance.
Leverage the probing tasks to find more linguistically-aware universal encoders.
papers.abstract: Although much effort has recently been devoted to training high-quality sentence embeddings, we still have a poor understanding of what they are capturing. "Downstream" tasks, often based on sentence classification, are commonly used to evaluate the quality of sentence representations. The complexity of the tasks makes it however difficult to infer what kind of information is present in the representations. We introduce here 10 probing tasks designed to capture simple linguistic features of sentences, and we use them to study embeddings generated by three different encoders trained in eight distinct ways, uncovering intriguing properties of both encoders and training methods.

papers.title: Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature to Reduce Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How is verbal uncertainty represented in LLMs, and can calibrating it with semantic uncertainty detect and mitigate hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that verbal uncertainty in LLMs is mediated by a linear feature (VUF) and introduces Mechanistic Uncertainty Calibration (MUC) to calibrate verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by ~30%.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that verbal uncertainty is a linear feature in LLMs, and calibrating it with semantic uncertainty through MUC effectively reduces confident hallucinations, making LLMs more trustworthy.
papers.key_findings:
Verbal uncertainty in LLMs is governed by a single linear direction (VUF) in the representation space, extractable via difference-in-means.
The mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone.
Inference-time intervention on VUF (MUC) calibrates verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by an average of 29.6% in short-form QA tasks.
VUFs are consistent across different datasets and models, indicating a universal feature.
MUC improves the alignment between verbal and semantic uncertainty, as shown by increased correlation coefficients.
papers.limitation: The method may reduce correctness rate due to noise in semantic uncertainty measurement, leading to unnecessary abstentions.
papers.abstract: LLMs often adopt an assertive language style also when making false claims. Such ``overconfident hallucinations'' mislead users and erode trust. Achieving the ability to express in language the actual degree of uncertainty around a claim is therefore of great importance. We find that ``verbal uncertainty'' is governed by a single linear feature in the representation space of LLMs, and show that this has only moderate correlation with the actual ``semantic uncertainty'' of the model. We apply this insight and show that (1) the mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone and (2) we can intervene on verbal uncertainty at inference time and reduce confident hallucinations on short-form answers, achieving an average relative reduction of ~30%.

papers.title: Cross-modal Associations in Vision and Language Models: Revisiting the Bouba-Kiki Effect
papers.research_question: Do vision-and-language models (VLMs) exhibit human-like cross-modal associations, specifically the bouba-kiki effect?
papers.core_contribution: CLIP models (ResNet and ViT) do not show consistent human-like cross-modal associations (bouba-kiki effect), and their internal representations lack the robust modality integration seen in humans.
papers.conclusion: VLMs do not exhibit human-like cross-modal associations, highlighting limitations in their internal representations and alignment with human intuitions.
papers.key_findings:
Neither CLIP ResNet nor ViT consistently exhibit the bouba-kiki effect across different prompts and pseudoword sets.
Models can correctly associate English adjectives with corresponding shapes (baseline), but fail for pseudowords.
Grad-CAM analysis shows that models do not attend to shape-specific features when processing pseudowords.
Models' predictions are inconsistent and often collapse to a few labels, indicating lack of robust cross-modal associations.
The models' performance is at chance level for the bouba-kiki task, in contrast to humans who show strong preferences.
papers.limitation:
Only tested on CLIP versions, not on more capable proprietary models.
Relies on text (orthographic) presentation of pseudowords, which may not capture auditory aspects of the bouba-kiki effect.
future_direction: Exploring cross-modal associations in more contemporary models (e.g., those with alignment layers).
Investigating audio-visual models to understand how different modalities contribute.
Incorporating cross-linguistic studies to account for cultural variation.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal models have raised questions about whether vision-and-language models (VLMs) integrate cross-modal information in ways that reflect human cognition. One well-studied test case in this domain is the bouba-kiki effect, where humans reliably associate pseudowords like `bouba' with round shapes and `kiki' with jagged ones. Given the mixed evidence found in prior studies for this effect in VLMs, we present a comprehensive re-evaluation focused on two variants of CLIP, ResNet and Vision Transformer (ViT), given their centrality in many state-of-the-art VLMs. We apply two complementary methods closely modelled after human experiments: a prompt-based evaluation that uses probabilities as a measure of model preference, and we use Grad-CAM as a novel approach to interpret visual attention in shape-word matching tasks. Our findings show that these model variants do not consistently exhibit the bouba-kiki effect. While ResNet shows a preference for round shapes, overall performance across both model variants lacks the expected associations. Moreover, direct comparison with prior human data on the same task shows that the models' responses fall markedly short of the robust, modality-integrated behaviour characteristic of human cognition. These results contribute to the ongoing debate about the extent to which VLMs truly understand cross-modal concepts, highlighting limitations in their internal representations and alignment with human intuitions.

papers.title: Visualizing and Understanding Neural Models in NLP
papers.research_question: How do neural models achieve compositionality, building sentence meaning from the meanings of words and phrases?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces visualization strategies, including representation plotting and first-derivative saliency, to understand how neural models compose meaning, revealing phenomena like negation asymmetry and the superior focus of LSTMs on key words.
papers.conclusion: The proposed visualization methods offer initial insights into how neural models achieve meaning composition in NLP tasks, explaining aspects of LSTM performance and revealing semantic properties like negation asymmetry.
papers.key_findings:
LSTMs and Bi-LSTMs show a sharper focus on important keywords (like 'hate') compared to standard RNNs, filtering out irrelevant information.
The models capture the linguistic property of negative asymmetry, where 'not bad' is clustered with negative words rather than positive ones.
In concessive sentences, the models operate competitively, with the stronger clause dominating the final sentiment representation.
First-derivative saliency can identify which input words contribute most to a classification decision, though it is an approximation and may not capture all non-linear interactions.
Sequence-to-sequence autoencoders implicitly learn alignments, linking words to be predicted back to corresponding regions in the input.
papers.limitation:
First-derivative saliency is a rough approximation and might not suffice to deal with highly non-linear cases, as it does not capture all the information needed for visualization.
The variance-based salience measure can only be used in scenarios where word embeddings are parameters to learn from scratch.
The attempts only touch superficial points in neural models.
future_direction: Using the results of visualization to perform error analysis.
Understanding the strengths and limitations of different neural models.
papers.abstract: While neural networks have been successfully applied to many NLP tasks the resulting vectorbased models are very difficult to interpret. For example it's not clear how they achieve compositionality, building sentence meaning from the meanings of words and phrases. In this paper we describe strategies for visualizing compositionality in neural models for NLP, inspired by similar work in computer vision. We first plot unit values to visualize compositionality of negation, intensification, and concessive clauses, allowing us to see wellknown markedness asymmetries in negation. We then introduce methods for visualizing a unit's salience, the amount that it contributes to the final composed meaning from first-order derivatives. Our general-purpose methods may have wide applications for understanding compositionality and other semantic properties of deep networks.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Visual Grounding: Different Effects for Speech- and Text-based Language Encoders
papers.research_question: How does visual grounding affect word representations in speech-based versus text-based language encoders?
papers.core_contribution: Visual grounding improves alignment between speech and text representations by enhancing word identity encoding, but it does not improve semantic discriminability in speech-based models and can even degrade it, contrasting with text-based models where semantic clustering is enhanced.
papers.conclusion: Visual grounding aligns representations of spoken and written language but enhances word identity rather than meaning, and it does not improve semantic discriminability in speech-based models, unlike in text-based models.
papers.key_findings:
Visual grounding increases similarity between speech- and text-based models, primarily by enhancing word identity representation.
In speech-based models, visual grounding does not improve semantic clustering and can disrupt pre-existing semantic structuring.
In text-based models, visual grounding improves semantic clustering.
Phonetic clustering remains similar in speech models with visual grounding.
The effect of visual grounding on clustering is influenced by word concreteness.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on intrinsic evaluations without examining downstream task performance.
future_direction: Relating differences in model-internal geometry to downstream task performance.
Developing visual grounding methods that target semantically relevant dimensions in middle layers of speech-based models.
papers.abstract: How does visual information included in training affect language processing in audio- and text-based deep learning models? We explore how such visual grounding affects model-internal representations of words, and find substantially different effects in speech- vs. text-based language encoders. Firstly, global representational comparisons reveal that visual grounding increases alignment between representations of spoken and written language, but this effect seems mainly driven by enhanced encoding of word identity rather than meaning. We then apply targeted clustering analyses to probe for phonetic vs. semantic discriminability in model representations. Speech-based representations remain phonetically dominated with visual grounding, but in contrast to text-based representations, visual grounding does not improve semantic discriminability. Our findings could usefully inform the development of more efficient methods to enrich speech-based models with visually-informed semantics.

papers.title: Constituency Parsing with a Self-Attentive Encoder
papers.research_question: How can self-attention be used for constituency parsing?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a constituency parsing model based on self-attention that achieves state-of-the-art results on the Penn Treebank and Chinese Treebank.
papers.conclusion: Self-attention is an effective mechanism for constituency parsing, providing both high performance and interpretable attention patterns.
papers.key_findings:
The self-attention parser achieves high F1 scores, outperforming previous recurrent and convolutional models.
Attention heads in the model capture syntactic relationships such as subject-verb dependencies.
The model demonstrates the effectiveness of self-attention for syntactic parsing tasks.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that replacing an LSTM encoder with a self-attentive architecture can lead to improvements to a state-ofthe-art discriminative constituency parser. The use of attention makes explicit the manner in which information is propagated between different locations in the sentence, which we use to both analyze our model and propose potential improvements. For example, we find that separating positional and content information in the encoder can lead to improved parsing accuracy. Additionally, we evaluate different approaches for lexical representation. Our parser achieves new state-ofthe-art results for single models trained on the Penn Treebank: 93.55 F1 without the use of any external data, and 95.13 F1 when using pre-trained word representations. Our parser also outperforms the previous best-published accuracy figures on 8 of the 9 languages in the SPMRL dataset.

papers.title: Two Effects, One Trigger: On the Modality Gap, Object Bias, and Information Imbalance in Contrastive Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the causes and effects of the modality gap and object bias in contrastive vision-language models, and can they be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that information imbalance between images and captions is the common cause of the modality gap and object bias in contrastive vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that information imbalance between modalities is the fundamental cause of the modality gap and object bias, and reducing this imbalance can mitigate these issues.
papers.key_findings:
For off-the-shelf VLMs, a larger modality gap correlates with better performance due to confounders, but controlling for confounders suggests a lower gap correlates with better performance.
Only few embedding dimensions drive the modality gap.
Image and text embeddings have distinct characteristics, like different neighborhood orderings.
Object bias does not negatively correlate with performance on attribute tasks.
Information imbalance between the modalities leads to both the modality gap and the object bias.
papers.limitation:
Validated on small- and medium-sized datasets; large-scale experiments are beyond computational resources.
The method of reducing information imbalance on real data may not be optimal.
Correlation-based results lack statistical significance due to small number of models.
future_direction: Developing data filtering or caption enrichment strategies to reduce information imbalance.
Transferring ideas from partial multi-label learning to CLIP-like models.
papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models (VLMs), like CLIP, have gained popularity for their versatile applicability to various downstream tasks. Despite their successes in some tasks, like zero-shot object recognition, they perform surprisingly poor on other tasks, like attribute recognition. Previous work has attributed these challenges to the modality gap, a separation of image and text in the shared representation space, and to a bias towards objects over other factors, such as attributes. In this analysis paper, we investigate both phenomena thoroughly. We evaluated off-the-shelf VLMs and while the gap's influence on performance is typically overshadowed by other factors, we find indications that closing the gap indeed leads to improvements. Moreover, we find that, contrary to intuition, only few embedding dimensions drive the gap and that the embedding spaces are differently organized. To allow for a clean study of object bias, we introduce a definition and a corresponding measure of it. Equipped with this tool, we find that object bias does not lead to worse performance on other concepts, such as attributes per se. However, why do both phenomena, modality gap and object bias, emerge in the first place? To answer this fundamental question and uncover some of the inner workings of contrastive VLMs, we conducted experiments that allowed us to control the amount of shared information between the modalities. These experiments revealed that the driving factor behind both the modality gap and the object bias, is an information imbalance between images and captions, and unveiled an intriguing connection between the modality gap and entropy of the logits.

papers.title: Extracting Visual Facts from Intermediate Layers for Mitigating Hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does prior knowledge in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suppress visual factual knowledge at the intermediate layer stage, and how can this be leveraged to mitigate object hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EV A, a training-free decoding method that dynamically selects intermediate layers with rich visual factual knowledge, contrasts their output distributions from multimodal and text-only inputs to extract this knowledge, and integrates it into the final layer to correct hallucinatory outputs.
papers.conclusion: EV A, a train-free decoding method that revises final outputs by extracting visual factual knowledge from intermediate layers, significantly reduces the incidence of hallucinations in MLLMs, highlighting its effectiveness.
papers.key_findings:
Visual factual knowledge and the Jensen-Shannon divergence between intermediate-layer original/prior probability distributions show similar evolutionary trends.
The intermediate layer with the maximum JS divergence contains richer visual factual knowledge.
EV A significantly reduces hallucination rates on benchmarks (POPE, MME, CHAIR) compared to baseline methods like DoLa, VCD, OPERA, and DeCo.
EV A is model-agnostic and seamlessly integrates with various classic decoding strategies (greedy search, nucleus sampling, beam search).
EV A's mechanism of subtracting LLM priors can lead to a decline in the model's original recognition capabilities on some tasks.
papers.limitation: Due to GPU cost constraints, experiments are exclusively conducted on a limited set of MLLMs, without exploring additional models or those with larger parameter scales.
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made significant strides by combining visual recognition and language understanding to generate content that is both coherent and contextually accurate. However, MLLMs continue to struggle with object hallucinations, where models produce seemingly plausible but factually incorrect outputs, including objects that do not exist in the image. Recent work has revealed that the prior knowledge in MLLMs significantly suppresses visual information in deep layers, causing hallucinatory outputs. However, how these priors suppress visual information at the intermediate layer stage in MLLMs remains unclear. We observe that visual factual knowledge and the differences between intermediate-layer prior/original probability distributions show similar evolutionary trends in intermediate layers. Motivated by this, we introduce Decoding by Extracting Visual Facts (EVA), a simple, training-free method that dynamically selects intermediate layers with the most significant visual factual information. By contrasting the output distributions of the selected layer derived from the original input and pure-text input, EVA extracts visual factual knowledge and proportionally incorporates it into the final layer to correct the output logits. Importantly, EVA is model-agnostic, seamlessly integrates with various classic decoding strategies, and is applicable across different MLLMs. We validate EVA on widely-used benchmarks, and the results show that it significantly reduces hallucination rates compared to baseline methods, underscoring its effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations.

papers.title: When Seeing Overrides Knowing: Disentangling Knowledge Conflicts in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do vision-language models resolve conflicts between their internal parametric knowledge and external visual information?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a dataset for analyzing knowledge conflicts in VLMs and identifies a small set of attention heads that mediate the conflict, showing that targeted interventions on these heads can steer the model's predictions.
papers.conclusion: The findings contribute to a deeper mechanistic understanding of how VLMs integrate and arbitrate between conflicting sources of information.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset of attention heads mediates the competition between factual and counterfactual predictions.
Attention blocks tend to support counterfactual information, while MLP blocks promote internal knowledge.
Counterfactual heads attend more to image tokens than factual heads.
Targeted interventions on these heads can shift the model's predictions towards either internal knowledge or visual context.
Attention-based attribution from these heads identifies counterfactual image regions more precisely than gradient-based methods.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is not a ready-to-deploy solution for mitigating hallucinations.
High intervention strengths can degrade the quality of generated text.
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly leverage diverse knowledge sources to address complex tasks, often encountering conflicts between their internal parametric knowledge and external information. Knowledge conflicts can result in hallucinations and unreliable responses, but the mechanisms governing such interactions remain unknown. To address this gap, we analyze the mechanisms that VLMs use to resolve cross-modal conflicts by introducing a dataset of multimodal counterfactual queries that deliberately contradict internal commonsense knowledge. We localize with logit inspection a small set of heads that control the conflict. Moreover, by modifying these heads, we can steer the model towards its internal knowledge or the visual inputs. Finally, we show that attention from such heads pinpoints localized image regions driving visual overrides, outperforming gradient-based attribution in precision.

papers.title: Can VLMs Recall Factual Associations From Visual References?
papers.research_question: Do VLMs have a systematic deficiency in recalling factual associations from visual references compared to textual references?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs exhibit a systematic deficiency in recalling factual knowledge from visual references compared to textual references, and this failure can be detected with high accuracy using linear probes on hidden states.
papers.conclusion: VLMs have a multimodal grounding gap that makes them struggle to link visual representations to internal knowledge, and probes on hidden states can help identify such failures; addressing this gap is important for future research.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs show a significant performance drop (over 50% on average) when forced to rely on visual references compared to textual references for factual recall.
This grounding gap persists across different model families, scales, and datasets.
Hidden state patterns differ between successful and failed linking cases, with failures building confidence later in the network.
Linear probes on hidden states can detect linking failures with over 92% accuracy and generalize to out-of-domain datasets.
Using these probes for selective prediction increases coverage by 7.87% and reduces error risk by 0.9% on OKVQA.
papers.limitation:
The work focuses exclusively on VLMs, leaving open whether similar gaps exist in other multimodal LMs (e.g., audio language models).
The paper does not address mitigating linking failure during VLM training.
The paper does not identify which particular design decision leads to the grounding gap.
future_direction: Expand feature-alignment pretraining to include factual recall tasks to improve grounding.
Investigate the grounding gap in other multimodal LMs (e.g., audio language models).
Identify which particular design decision leads to the grounding gap.
papers.abstract: Through a controlled study, we identify a systematic deficiency in the multimodal grounding of Vision Language Models (VLMs). While VLMs can recall factual associations when provided a textual reference to an entity; their ability to do so is significantly diminished when the reference is visual instead. Forcing VLMs to rely on image representations of an entity halves their ability to recall factual knowledge, suggesting that VLMs struggle to link their internal knowledge of an entity with its image representation. We show that such linking failures are correlated with the expression of distinct patterns in model internal states, and that probes on these internal states achieve over 92% accuracy at flagging cases where the VLM response is unreliable. These probes can be applied, without retraining, to identify when a VLM will fail to correctly answer a question that requires an understanding of multimodal input. When used to facilitate selective prediction on a visual question answering task, the probes increase coverage by 7.87% (absolute) while also reducing the risk of error by 0.9% (absolute). Addressing the systematic, detectable deficiency is an important avenue in language grounding, and we provide informed recommendations for future directions.

papers.title: Understanding Neural Networks through Representation Erasure
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural network decisions by analyzing the effects of erasing various parts of the representation, such as input word-vector dimensions, intermediate hidden units, or input words?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a general methodology for interpreting neural network decisions by erasing parts of the representation and analyzing the effects, which provides explanations for model behavior and enables error analysis.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methodology offers interpretable explanations for neural model decisions and provides a way to conduct error analysis, which can benefit a wide variety of models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The method identifies important word-vector dimensions for linguistic feature classification and shows how importance distributes across dimensions and layers.
In sentiment analysis, LSTM-based models are more sensitive to sentiment-indicative words than standard RNNs.
The method can identify words that confuse the model (negative importance) and reveal common failure patterns, such as sentiment words used in non-standard contexts.
A reinforcement learning approach can find minimal sets of words to erase to change model decisions, providing aspect-specific rationales.
Dropout training leads to more distributed importance across dimensions.
future_direction: Resolving the problems identified in error analysis (e.g., handling concessive sentences, irony, etc.) in sentiment analysis.
papers.abstract: While neural networks have been successfully applied to many natural language processing tasks, they come at the cost of interpretability. In this paper, we propose a general methodology to analyze and interpret decisions from a neural model by observing the effects on the model of erasing various parts of the representation, such as input word-vector dimensions, intermediate hidden units, or input words. We present several approaches to analyzing the effects of such erasure, from computing the relative difference in evaluation metrics, to using reinforcement learning to erase the minimum set of input words in order to flip a neural model's decision. In a comprehensive analysis of multiple NLP tasks, including linguistic feature classification, sentence-level sentiment analysis, and document level sentiment aspect prediction, we show that the proposed methodology not only offers clear explanations about neural model decisions, but also provides a way to conduct error analysis on neural models.

papers.title: Neural Mechanisms Underlying Visual Object Recognition
papers.research_question: How does the brain achieve invariant visual object recognition? The paper seeks to build falsifiable, predictive models of the encoding (from images to neural activity) and decoding (from neural activity to behavior) processes underlying core object recognition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper builds predictive models of the neural mechanisms for visual object recognition: a hierarchical neural network (HMO) optimized for object recognition performance predicts neural responses in V4 and IT cortex, and a simple linear decoder from IT neural activity accurately predicts human behavior across many object recognition tasks.
papers.conclusion: Core object recognition is largely supported by a feed-forward cascade of neural activity, with encoding via a hierarchical nonlinear network and decoding via a simple linear readout from IT cortex.
papers.key_findings:
A simple linear decoder from IT neural population activity accurately predicts human object recognition behavior across a wide range of tasks.
Inactivation of face-selective IT subregions causally impairs face gender discrimination, and the impairment correlates with local linear separability of neural responses.
Hierarchical convolutional neural networks optimized for object recognition performance predict neural responses in V4 and IT cortex.
The HMO model achieves near-human performance on object categorization and explains a large fraction of neural response variance.
Combining the encoding (HMO) and decoding (linear) models provides an end-to-end mechanistic model of core object recognition.
papers.limitation:
The encoding and decoding models are imperfect and do not capture all of the variance in neural responses and behavior.
Only a subset of possible behavioral tasks has been explored, leaving open the possibility of failure on other tasks.
The origin of cortical heterogeneity (e.g., spatial clustering of face-selective neurons) and the functional significance of multiple cortical layers in each visual area are not explained.
The role of feedback circuits in complex visual behaviors (e.g., visual memory, learning, top-down inference) is not addressed.
future_direction: Extend causal methods to a battery of object recognition tests and build stronger quantitative links between neural activity and behavior.
Understand the role of feedback circuits in complex visual behaviors involving visual memory, learning, top-down inference, and sensorimotor integration over extended time periods.
papers.abstract: Invariant visual object recognition and the underlying neural representations are fundamental to higher-level human cognition. To understand these neural underpinnings, we combine human and monkey psychophysics, large-scale neurophysiology, neural perturbation methods, and computational modeling to construct falsifiable, predictive models that aim to fully account for the neural encoding and decoding processes that underlie visual object recognition. A predictive encoding model must minimally describe the transformation of the retinal image to population patterns of neural activity along the entire cortical ventral stream of visual processing and must accurately predict the responses to any retinal image. A predictive decoding model must minimally describe the transformation from those population patterns of neural activity to observed object recognition behavior (i.e., subject reports), and, given that population pattern of activity, it must accurately predict behavior for any object recognition task. To date, we have focused on core object recognition-a remarkable behavior that is accomplished with image viewing durations of <200 msec.
