The framework demonstrates that neural networks can learn representations that are linear transformations of true physical quantities (e.g., forces) when appropriate inductive biases are applied.
The approach offers a pathway to interpret neural networks and discover novel physical principles from the representations they learn.
future_direction: Extending the framework to gridded PDE data using existing symbolic regression packages for PDEs.
Using other symbolic regression packages (e.g., PySR, grammar-based methods) as drop-in replacements for eureqa in the framework.
papers.abstract: We develop a general approach to distill symbolic representations of a learned deep model by introducing strong inductive biases. We focus on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The technique works as follows: we first encourage sparse latent representations when we train a GNN in a supervised setting, then we apply symbolic regression to components of the learned model to extract explicit physical relations. We find the correct known equations, including force laws and Hamiltonians, can be extracted from the neural network. We then apply our method to a non-trivial cosmology example-a detailed dark matter simulation-and discover a new analytic formula which can predict the concentration of dark matter from the mass distribution of nearby cosmic structures. The symbolic expressions extracted from the GNN using our technique also generalized to out-of-distribution data better than the GNN itself. Our approach offers alternative directions for interpreting neural networks and discovering novel physical principles from the representations they learn.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Like Internally
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether surprisal (negative log probability) from internal layers of large language models aligns with human sentence processing data, and whether the alignment varies by layer depth and the type of human measure (behavioral vs. neurophysiological).
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that surprisal from internal layers of larger language models aligns well with human sentence processing data, challenging prior conclusions that focused on final layers. Additionally, it finds that earlier layers align with fast human measures (e.g., gaze duration) and later layers with slower measures (e.g., N400).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that larger language models are cognitively plausible when internal layers are considered, and that different layers correspond to different stages of human sentence processing, advocating for layer-wise alignment in cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal from internal layers of larger LMs aligns with human sentence processing data as well as or better than smaller LMs.
The last layer does not yield the best alignment; the best layer varies by human measure.
Earlier layers align better with fast human measures (e.g., first-pass gaze duration, self-paced reading time), while later layers align better with slower measures (e.g., N400, MAZE processing time).
When considering the best internal layer, larger LMs show a positive scaling effect (larger models have higher ∆LL) for most human measures.
The alignment patterns are consistent across multiple languages (tested on MECO corpus).
papers.limitation: The study is focused on naturalistic reading corpora and does not include controlled experiments on syntactic ambiguity or grammatical violation, which are known challenges for surprisal theory.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other probability-based measures such as entropy and entropy reduction.
Combine the internal layer approach with linguistically-motivated neural models.
papers.abstract: Recent cognitive modeling studies have reported that larger language models (LMs) exhibit a poorer fit to human reading behavior (Oh and Schuler, 2023b; Shain et al., 2024; Kuribayashi et al., 2024), leading to claims of their cognitive implausibility. In this paper, we revisit this argument through the lens of mechanistic interpretability and argue that prior conclusions were skewed by an exclusive focus on the final layers of LMs. Our analysis reveals that next-word probabilities derived from internal layers of larger LMs align with human sentence processing data as well as, or better than, those from smaller LMs. This alignment holds consistently across behavioral (self-paced reading times, gaze durations, MAZE task processing times) and neurophysiological (N400 brain potentials) measures, challenging earlier mixed results and suggesting that the cognitive plausibility of larger LMs has been underestimated. Furthermore, we first identify an intriguing relationship between LM layers and human measures: earlier layers correspond more closely with fast gaze durations, while later layers better align with relatively slower signals such as N400 potentials and MAZE processing times. Our work opens new avenues for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and cognitive modeling.

papers.title: Reconstruction-guided attention improves the robustness and shape processing of neural networks
papers.research_question: How does using object reconstruction as top-down attentional feedback improve the robustness of object recognition models against image corruptions?
papers.core_contribution: Introducing reconstruction-guided attention, which uses object reconstruction as top-down feedback, improves the robustness of neural networks to image corruptions and provides insights into human visual processing.
papers.conclusion: Reconstruction-guided attention improves robustness to image corruptions by using object reconstruction as top-down feedback, with spatial masking enhancing classification accuracy and feature binding improving inference efficiency, offering insights into human visual processing.
papers.key_findings:
The model with reconstruction-guided attention outperforms baseline CNNs and CapsNet on the MNIST-C benchmark, especially on shape-related corruptions like blur, noise, and occlusion.
Ablation studies show that the reconstruction-based spatial mask significantly improves classification accuracy, while the reconstruction-based feature binding mainly reduces inference time (number of steps to reach confidence).
The model sometimes hallucinates non-existing patterns from noise, producing human-like errors.
Even low-resolution object reconstruction is sufficient to improve robustness, consistent with human use of low spatial frequency information.
The model does not suffer from overfitting when using a higher capacity encoder (Resnet-18), unlike simple CNNs.
papers.limitation: The model is only evaluated on digit recognition and not on more naturalistic images.
future_direction: Apply the model to other datasets and tasks beyond digit recognition to understand the broader role of object reconstruction in robust visual perception.
Collect human recognition responses through psychophysical experiments to compare model behavior with humans.
papers.abstract: Many visual phenomena suggest that humans use top-down generative or reconstructive processes to create visual percepts (e.g., imagery, object completion, pareidolia), but little is known about the role reconstruction plays in robust object recognition. We built an iterative encoder-decoder network that generates an object reconstruction and used it as top-down attentional feedback to route the most relevant spatial and feature information to feed-forward object recognition processes. We tested this model using the challenging out-of-distribution digit recognition dataset, MNIST-C, where 15 different types of transformation and corruption are applied to handwritten digit images. Our model showed strong generalization performance against various image perturbations, on average outperforming all other models including feedforward CNNs and adversarially trained networks. Our model is particularly robust to blur, noise, and occlusion corruptions, where shape perception plays an important role. Ablation studies further reveal two complementary roles of spatial and feature-based attention in robust object recognition, with the former largely consistent with spatial masking benefits in the attention literature (the reconstruction serves as a mask) and the latter mainly contributing to the model's inference speed (i.e., number of time steps to reach a certain confidence threshold) by reducing the space of possible object hypotheses. We also observed that the model sometimes hallucinates a non-existing pattern out of noise, leading to highly interpretable human-like errors. Our study shows that modeling reconstruction-based feedback endows AI systems with a powerful attention mechanism, which can help us understand the role of generating perception in human visual processing.

papers.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
papers.research_question: How can conditional computation be realized to dramatically increase model capacity without a proportional increase in computation, specifically for language modeling and machine translation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts layer that enables conditional computation, achieving over 1000x increase in model capacity with minimal computational efficiency loss, and advances state-of-the-art on language modeling and machine translation benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The Sparsely-Gated MoE layer successfully realizes the promise of conditional computation, enabling massive increases in model capacity with minimal computational overhead, and achieves state-of-the-art results on language modeling and machine translation.
papers.key_findings:
The MoE layer with up to thousands of experts can be trained efficiently using the proposed gating and load balancing techniques.
On the 1-Billion-Word benchmark, MoE models achieve significantly lower perplexity than LSTMs with similar computational budgets.
On a 100-billion-word corpus, MoE models with up to 68 billion parameters in the MoE layer achieve 39% lower perplexity than a baseline LSTM.
On WMT translation tasks, MoE-augmented models achieve higher BLEU scores than strong baselines with less computation.
The experts in the MoE layer become specialized to specific syntactic and semantic contexts.
papers.limitation:
Performance degrades with 131072 experts, possibly due to too much sparsity.
The approach is focused on text and may require sufficiently large training sets for other domains.
future_direction: Application of conditional computation to other domains beyond text.
Further exploration of novel implementations and applications of conditional computation.
papers.abstract: The capacity of a neural network to absorb information is limited by its number of parameters. Conditional computation, where parts of the network are active on a per-example basis, has been proposed in theory as a way of dramatically increasing model capacity without a proportional increase in computation. In practice, however, there are significant algorithmic and performance challenges. In this work, we address these challenges and finally realize the promise of conditional computation, achieving greater than 1000x improvements in model capacity with only minor losses in computational efficiency on modern GPU clusters. We introduce a Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts layer (MoE), consisting of up to thousands of feed-forward sub-networks. A trainable gating network determines a sparse combination of these experts to use for each example. We apply the MoE to the tasks of language modeling and machine translation, where model capacity is critical for absorbing the vast quantities of knowledge available in the training corpora. We present model architectures in which a MoE with up to 137 billion parameters is applied convolutionally between stacked LSTM layers. On large language modeling and machine translation benchmarks, these models achieve significantly better results than state-of-the-art at lower computational cost.

papers.title: The Tensor Brain: Semantic Decoding for Perception and Memory
papers.research_question: How can perception and memory be modeled using tensor models and knowledge graphs, and what insights does this provide into the human mind?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a tensor-based mathematical model for perception and memory, proposing a four-layer complex semantic decoder (sensory memory, representation, index, and working memory) that integrates sensory input with semantic and episodic memory to generate explicit triple statements.
papers.conclusion: The tensor brain model offers a comprehensive mathematical framework for understanding perception and memory, connecting to established cognitive theories and demonstrating strong experimental results on visual relationship benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed tensor model with a four-layer semantic decoder provides a unified framework for perception and memory, linking to cognitive theories like global workspace and Bayesian brain.
The complex semantic decoder, which includes working memory, significantly improves performance on visual relationship detection tasks compared to simpler decoders.
The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets (Visual Genome and VRD) for visual relationship detection.
Semantic memory acts as a prior distribution for triple statements, complementing sensory input and improving decoding accuracy.
The model suggests that explicit perception and declarative memory require working memory and may be unique to humans, enabling complex language and reasoning.
future_direction: Integration of language production capabilities into the model.
Extension to more complex reasoning and planning tasks.
Incorporation of more complex neural architectures and larger-scale datasets.
papers.abstract: We analyse perception and memory, using mathematical models for knowledge graphs and tensors, to gain insights into the corresponding functionalities of the human mind. Our discussion is based on the concept of propositional sentences consisting of \textit{subject-predicate-object} (SPO) triples for expressing elementary facts. SPO sentences are the basis for most natural languages but might also be important for explicit perception and declarative memories, as well as intra-brain communication and the ability to argue and reason. A set of SPO sentences can be described as a knowledge graph, which can be transformed into an adjacency tensor. We introduce tensor models, where concepts have dual representations as indices and associated embeddings, two constructs we believe are essential for the understanding of implicit and explicit perception and memory in the brain. We argue that a biological realization of perception and memory imposes constraints on information processing. In particular, we propose that explicit perception and declarative memories require a semantic decoder, which, in a simple realization, is based on four layers: First, a sensory memory layer, as a buffer for sensory input, second, an index layer representing concepts, third, a memoryless representation layer for the broadcasting of information ---the "blackboard", or the "canvas" of the brain--- and fourth, a working memory layer as a processing center and data buffer. We discuss the operations of the four layers and relate them to the global workspace theory. In a Bayesian brain interpretation, semantic memory defines the prior for observable triple statements. We propose that ---in evolution and during development--- semantic memory, episodic memory, and natural language evolved as emergent properties in agents' process to gain a deeper understanding of sensory information.

papers.title: Analyzing the Roles of Language and Vision in Learning from Limited Data
papers.research_question: How do language and vision contribute to learning from limited data in vision-language models? Specifically, what are the roles of visual processing, prior knowledge, and reasoning in visual understanding?
papers.core_contribution: A language model with prior knowledge, reasoning, and a few examples recovers over 75% of a vision-language model's performance on visual tasks without visual input, indicating language provides substantial visual understanding through knowledge and reasoning.
papers.conclusion: A language model with prior knowledge, reasoning, and examples can recover a majority of a VLM's visual understanding performance, and all three language components are necessary. Vision models without language underperform compared to full language models.
papers.key_findings:
Removing visual processing but retaining language components (prior knowledge, reasoning, examples) maintains just over 75% of the VLM's performance.
Each language component (prior knowledge, reasoning, examples) is necessary; ablating any one significantly reduces performance.
A vision-only model with knowledge but no reasoning achieves about half the performance of the VLM, comparable to a language model missing one component.
Removing prior knowledge from the vision-only model reduces performance to random chance.
The synergy of all three language components is required for high performance in the absence of vision.
papers.limitation:
The text used as language input (image tags) was obtained from the image's source rather than annotated, so they vary in descriptiveness.
Evaluations are solely on GPT models due to the closed nature of their architecture and training data.
The pre-trained image model (ResNet50) is smaller than the VLM and uses a much smaller dataset, which may limit its performance and underestimate the contribution of prior knowledge in the vision case.
future_direction: Explore collecting new tags via crowdsourcing processes like STEP-Tag or by using a VLM.
Repeat experiments on open-source models such as LLaMA and LLaVA.
Find or train image models on comparable amounts of data to further investigate hypotheses.
papers.abstract: Does language help make sense of the visual world? How important is it to actually see the world rather than having it described with words? These basic questions about the nature of intelligence have been difficult to answer because we only had one example of an intelligent system -- humans -- and limited access to cases that isolated language or vision. However, the development of sophisticated Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by artificial intelligence researchers offers us new opportunities to explore the contributions that language and vision make to learning about the world. We ablate components from the cognitive architecture of these models to identify their contributions to learning new tasks from limited data. We find that a language model leveraging all components recovers a majority of a VLM's performance, despite its lack of visual input, and that language seems to allow this by providing access to prior knowledge and reasoning.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Machine Learning Topological Invariants with Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can neural networks learn topological invariants from local inputs and generalize to predict winding numbers for Hamiltonians with larger winding numbers not seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that neural networks can successfully learn global topological invariants from local Hamiltonian inputs, generalize to predict winding numbers beyond the training range, and internally learn the discrete winding number formula.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn global and nonlinear topological features from local inputs and exhibit strong generalization power, opening possibilities for using machine learning to study topological physics.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can predict topological winding numbers with nearly 100% accuracy, even for Hamiltonians with larger winding numbers not included in the training data.
Convolutional networks outperform fully-connected networks due to their inherent translation symmetry, which matches the symmetry of the winding number problem.
By analyzing the internal function of the convolutional network, the authors confirm it learns the discrete version of the winding number formula.
Regularization techniques like L2 regularization can harm generalization when training data are noise-free, but become beneficial when noise is present.
If training data are restricted to a specific model (e.g., the SSH model), the network may learn shortcuts based on local symmetries and fail to generalize to more general Hamiltonians.
papers.limitation:
Regularization techniques can be detrimental to generalization when the training data are noise-free.
If the training data are restricted to a specific model with additional symmetries, the neural network may learn shortcuts and fail to generalize to more general cases.
future_direction: Generalize the results to topological models in higher dimensions and other symmetry classes.
Apply the trained network to analyze data from quantum simulators.
papers.abstract: In this Letter we supervisedly train neural networks to distinguish different topological phases in the context of topological band insulators. After training with Hamiltonians of one-dimensional insulators with chiral symmetry, the neural network can predict their topological winding numbers with nearly 100% accuracy, even for Hamiltonians with larger winding numbers that are not included in the training data. These results show a remarkable success that the neural network can capture the global and nonlinear topological features of quantum phases from local inputs. By opening up the neural network, we confirm that the network does learn the discrete version of the winding number formula. We also make a couple of remarks regarding the role of the symmetry and the opposite effect of regularization techniques when applying machine learning to physical systems.

papers.title: Integrated deep visual and semantic attractor neural networks predict fMRI pattern-information along the ventral object processing pathway
papers.research_question: How does visual processing activate and interact with semantic representations during object recognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines a deep convolutional neural network model of vision with an attractor network model of semantics and shows that different stages of this integrated model explain fMRI pattern-information along the ventral object processing pathway.
papers.conclusion: The combined visuo-semantic model provides a proof-of-principle for how visual and semantic processing can be integrated and accounts for neural data along the ventral stream, showing a gradient from visual to semantic representations.
papers.key_findings:
Visual layers of the DNN best explain activation patterns in early visual cortex.
Posterior ventral temporal cortex is best explained by early stages of the semantic attractor network, corresponding to initial semantic processing.
Perirhinal cortex is best explained by the final stages of the semantic attractor network, when detailed semantic representations are activated.
The model learns associations between high-level visual regularities and semantic features, with shared semantic features activating more rapidly than distinctive features.
The model implements a general-to-specific account of object processing, where coarse-grained semantics activate before fine-grained details.
papers.limitation:
The model is trained in two separate stages (pre-trained DNN then attractor network), so there is no possibility for semantic representations to influence earlier visual layers via feedback.
The model is trained and tested on a specific set of images and has not been evaluated on its ability to generalize semantic patterns to previously unseen images.
future_direction: Training the visual and semantic components of the model together in an end-to-end manner.
Exploring architectures with direct connections from early visual layers to semantics, semantic-to-visual top-down connections, and lateral recurrent connections within visual layers.
Testing the model's semantic patterns for previously unseen images.
papers.abstract: Recognising an object involves rapid visual processing and activation of semantic knowledge about the object, but how visual processing activates and interacts with semantic representations remains unclear. Cognitive neuroscience research has shown that while visual processing involves posterior regions along the ventral stream, object meaning involves more anterior regions, especially perirhinal cortex. Here we investigate visuo-semantic processing by combining a deep neural network model of vision with an attractor network model of semantics, such that visual information maps onto object meanings represented as activation patterns across features. In the combined model, concept activation is driven by visual input and co-occurrence of semantic features, consistent with neurocognitive accounts. We tested the model's ability to explain fMRI data where participants named objects. Visual layers explained activation patterns in early visual cortex, whereas pattern-information in perirhinal cortex was best explained by later stages of the attractor network, when detailed semantic representations are activated. Posterior ventral temporal cortex was best explained by intermediate stages corresponding to initial semantic processing, when visual information has the greatest influence on the emerging semantic representation. These results provide proof of principle of how a mechanistic model of combined visuo-semantic processing can account for pattern-information in the ventral stream.

papers.title: Anatomy of Catastrophic Forgetting: Hidden Representations and Task Semantics
papers.research_question: How does catastrophic forgetting affect the hidden representations of neural networks, and how is it influenced by task semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that catastrophic forgetting is primarily driven by changes in deeper layers, and that forgetting is most severe for tasks with intermediate semantic similarity.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that catastrophic forgetting is concentrated in higher layers, mitigation methods stabilize these layers, and forgetting is maximized for tasks of intermediate similarity, providing a foundation for understanding and mitigating forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Deeper layers are the primary source of forgetting in neural networks.
Forgetting mitigation methods like elastic weight consolidation and replay buffers act by stabilizing deeper layer representations.
Forgetting is most severe for tasks with intermediate semantic similarity.
Representational similarity (measured by CKA) between tasks is key to understanding forgetting.
A novel CIFAR-100 distribution shift task approximates realistic input distribution shift for studying forgetting.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in developing versatile machine learning systems is catastrophic forgetting: a model trained on tasks in sequence will suffer significant performance drops on earlier tasks. Despite the ubiquity of catastrophic forgetting, there is limited understanding of the underlying process and its causes. In this paper, we address this important knowledge gap, investigating how forgetting affects representations in neural network models. Through representational analysis techniques, we find that deeper layers are disproportionately the source of forgetting. Supporting this, a study of methods to mitigate forgetting illustrates that they act to stabilize deeper layers. These insights enable the development of an analytic argument and empirical picture relating the degree of forgetting to representational similarity between tasks. Consistent with this picture, we observe maximal forgetting occurs for task sequences with intermediate similarity. We perform empirical studies on the standard split CIFAR-10 setup and also introduce a novel CIFAR-100 based task approximating realistic input distribution shift.

papers.title: The attentive reconstruction of objects facilitates robust object recognition
papers.research_question: How does object reconstruction serve as top-down attention feedback to facilitate robust object recognition under conditions of noise and occlusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ORA, a model that uses object reconstruction as top-down attention feedback to bias feedforward processing, demonstrating improved robustness to noise/occlusion and better alignment with human reaction times and error patterns than standard CNNs.
papers.conclusion: Attentive reconstruction of objects is a plausible neural mechanism for achieving robust object perception and recognition, unifying spatial and feature-based attention into one computational system.
papers.key_findings:
ORA achieves superior recognition accuracy on corrupted digit (MNIST-C) and natural image (ImageNet-C) datasets compared to standard feedforward CNN baselines.
ORA's spatial masking mechanism is crucial for recognition accuracy, while its feature binding mechanism is important for recognition speed (number of iterations).
The number of forward processing steps ORA requires to reach a classification decision correlates with human reaction times on the same tasks.
ORA and human participants show similar patterns of recognition errors (digit confusions).
ORA's performance benefits are particularly pronounced on corruptions that affect object shape.
papers.limitation:
The high compression rate in ORA's decoder limits its ability to reconstruct fine-grained object details.
The model is evaluated on static images and single-object recognition, not on dynamic scenes or multiple objects.
future_direction: Extend ORA to object-based attention tasks involving multiple objects, such as perceptual grouping and multiple-object tracking.
Investigate the optimization of the information and level of object reconstruction for greater performance benefits.
Explore the use of advanced decoder architectures and composition-based methods to generate higher-quality reconstructions.
papers.abstract: Humans are extremely robust in our ability to perceive and recognize objects-we see faces in tea stains and can recognize friends on dark streets. Yet, neurocomputational models of primate object recognition have focused on the initial feed-forward pass of processing through the ventral stream and less on the top-down feedback that likely underlies robust object perception and recognition. Aligned with the generative approach, we propose that the visual system actively facilitates recognition by reconstructing the object hypothesized to be in the image. Top-down attention then uses this reconstruction as a template to bias feedforward processing to align with the most plausible object hypothesis. Building on auto-encoder neural networks, our model makes detailed hypotheses about the appearance and location of the candidate objects in the image by reconstructing a complete object representation from potentially incomplete visual input due to noise and occlusion. The model then leverages the best object reconstruction, measured by reconstruction error, to direct the bottom-up process of selectively routing low-level features, a top-down biasing that captures a core function of attention. We evaluated our model using the MNIST-C (handwritten digits under corruptions) and ImageNet-C (real-world objects under corruptions) datasets. Not only did our model achieve superior performance on these challenging tasks designed to approximate real-world noise and occlusion viewing conditions, but also better accounted for human behavioral reaction times and error patterns than a standard feedforward Convolutional Neural Network. Our model suggests that a complete understanding of object perception and recognition requires integrating top-down and attention feedback, which we propose is an object reconstruction.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: High-level visual representations in the human brain are aligned with large language models
papers.research_question: Here we test whether the contextual information encoded in large language models (LLMs) is beneficial for modelling the complex visual information extracted by the brain from natural scenes.
papers.core_contribution: LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully characterize brain activity evoked by natural scenes and provide a representational format that accounts for complex visual information extracted by the brain.
papers.conclusion: LLM embeddings provide a versatile representational format for capturing complex information derived by the brain from visual inputs, paving the way for new research avenues.
papers.key_findings:
LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully predict brain activity across higher-level visual areas.
Linear encoding and decoding models using LLM embeddings can capture region-specific tuning properties and reconstruct accurate scene captions from brain activity.
The alignment derives from LLMs' ability to integrate complex information beyond individual words or object categories.
ANNs trained to predict LLM embeddings from images learn representations better aligned with brain activity than many state-of-the-art models, despite less training data.
papers.limitation: The task of the NSD participants was to report if they had previously seen each presented image. It cannot be fully ruled out that, to perform this continuous recognition task, participants were internally captioning the scenes, and this may have benefitted the LLM caption embeddings as a good model of visual responses.
future_direction: Exploring datasets where prepositions, adjectives and adverbs play a more important role is an intriguing direction for future research.
An interesting future direction of research will spell out whether the rich learning signal derived from language might indeed provide important benefits over other training objectives.
It will be interesting for future work to investigate LLM-based codes under different tasks.
papers.abstract: The human brain extracts complex information from visual inputs, including objects, their spatial and semantic interrelations, and their interactions with the environment. However, a quantitative approach for studying this information remains elusive. Here we test whether the contextual information encoded in large language models (LLMs) is beneficial for modelling the complex visual information extracted by the brain from natural scenes. We show that LLM embeddings of scene captions successfully characterize brain activity evoked by viewing the natural scenes. This mapping captures selectivities of different brain areas and is sufficiently robust that accurate scene captions can be reconstructed from brain activity. Using carefully controlled model comparisons, we then proceed to show that the accuracy with which LLM representations match brain representations derives from the ability of LLMs to integrate complex information contained in scene captions beyond that conveyed by individual words. Finally, we train deep neural network models to transform image inputs into LLM representations. Remarkably, these networks learn representations that are better aligned with brain representations than a large number of state-of-the-art alternative models, despite being trained on orders-of-magnitude less data. Overall, our results suggest that LLM embeddings of scene captions provide a representational format that accounts for complex information extracted by the brain from visual inputs.

papers.title: A Neural Model of Episodic and Semantic Spatiotemporal Memory
papers.research_question: How can a neural network model form sparse spatiotemporal memory traces from single occurrences and achieve similarity-based generalization for semantic memory?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes TESMECOR, a neural network model that forms sparse distributed memory traces for spatiotemporal events from single occurrences, enabling similarity-based generalization for semantic memory.
papers.conclusion: TESMECOR exhibits both episodic memory and similarity-based generalization for semantic memory in the spatiotemporal domain, as demonstrated by simulations.
papers.key_findings:
The model exhibits high capacity for episodic spatiotemporal memory with single-trial learning.
TESMECOR achieves similarity-based generalization and categorization in the spatiotemporal pattern domain.
The noise-modulated internal representation selection scheme controls overlap between memory traces based on input similarity.
Simulation results show that the model can lock into correct memory traces for degraded inputs by the final time slice.
The model uses a continuous similarity measure G to inject noise, allowing for variable overlap between internal representations.
papers.limitation:
Accuracy on intermediate time slices can be low for highly degraded inputs, though final time slice accuracy is high.
The simulations are preliminary and not exhaustive.
future_direction: Incorporating a hippocampal component to provide additional evidence vectors to the L2 cells.
papers.abstract: A neural network model is proposed that forms sparse spatiotemporal memory traces of spatiotemporal events given single occurrences of the events.The traces are distributed in that each individual cell and synapse participates in numerous traces.This sharing of representational substrate provides the basis for similaritybased generalization and thus semantic memory.Simulation results are provided demonstrating that similar spatiotemporal patterns map to similar traces.The model achieves this property by measuring the degree of match, G, between the current input pattern on each time slice and the expected input given the preceding time slices (i.e., temporal context) and then adding an amount of noise, inversely proportional to G, to the process of choosing the internal representation for the current time slice.Thus, if G is small, indicating novelty, we add much noise and the resulting internal representation of the current input pattern has low overlap with any preexisting representations of time slices.If G is large, indicating a familiar event, we add very little noise resulting in reactivation of all or most of the preexisting representation of the input pattern.

papers.title: Attention weights accurately predict language representations in the brain
papers.research_question: Are attention weights in Transformer-based language models related to language representations in the brain? Can attention weights predict brain responses to language stimuli?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights from Transformer-based language models accurately predict brain responses in language-related cortical areas, and contain information not captured by lexical or contextual embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Attention weights in Transformer-based LMs capture information that is reflected in brain representations during language processing, and indicate cortical areas that could be involved in integrating context across words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 accurately predict brain responses in frontal and temporal cortices associated with language processing.
Attention weights better predict brain responses than lexical embeddings in many language-related areas.
Attention weights from middle layers of BERT explain the most variance in brain responses, consistent with linguistic relevance of middle layers.
Attention weights from BERT and GPT-2 perform similarly in predicting brain responses, suggesting consistency across unidirectional and bidirectional models.
In some cortical areas, attention weights predict brain responses better than contextual embeddings, indicating additional information in attention weights.
papers.limitation:
The temporal resolution of fMRI (2s) does not capture all the rapid changes in human speech.
Analyses were limited to English language comprehension.
The analyses demonstrate similarity of representations between Transformer-based LMs and brain responses, but do not directly prove the existence of similar underlying computational mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other languages to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of context integration in the brain and in artificial neural networks.

Compare the results of our method of computing attention weights with more cognitively-inspired methods to provide more specific insights into how attention weights in Transformer-based LMs relate to processes in the human brain.
papers.abstract: In Transformer-based language models (LMs) the attention mechanism converts token embeddings into contextual embeddings that incorporate information from neighboring words. The resulting contextual hidden state embeddings have enabled highly accurate models of brain responses, suggesting that the attention mechanism constructs contextual embeddings that carry information reflected in language-related brain representations. However, it is unclear whether the attention weights that are used to integrate information across words are themselves related to language representations in the brain. To address this question we analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings of participants reading English language narratives. We provided the narrative text as input to two LMs (BERT and GPT-2) and extracted their corresponding attention weights. We then used encoding models to determine how well attention weights can predict recorded brain responses. We find that attention weights accurately predict brain responses in much of the frontal and temporal cortices. Our results suggest that the attention mechanism itself carries information that is reflected in brain representations. Moreover, these results indicate cortical areas in which context integration may occur.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of layers in neural networks and how do learning dynamics evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that layers are over-parameterized, learning converges from bottom up, and proposes Freeze Training to save computation and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful tool for comparing learned representations across layers, architectures, and time, providing insights into learning dynamics and motivating new training and compression techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is often much smaller than the number of neurons, indicating over-parameterization.
Learning dynamics show that networks converge from the bottom up, with lower layers solidifying before higher ones.
SVCCA can capture semantic similarities between classes, with similar classes having similar sensitivity patterns in the network.
Freeze Training, which sequentially freezes lower layers during training, can save computation and sometimes improve generalization.
The important directions found by SVCCA are distributed across many neurons rather than being axis-aligned.
papers.abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: From phonemes to images: levels of representation in a recurrent neural\n model of visually-grounded language learning
papers.research_question: How does a recurrent neural model learn to predict visual features from phoneme sequences, and how are linguistic representations structured across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a phoneme-level recurrent neural model for visually-grounded language learning and demonstrates that it learns hierarchical representations where lower layers encode form and higher layers encode meaning.
papers.conclusion: The model learns hierarchical representations with lower layers encoding short-timescale form information and higher layers encoding meaning, providing a step towards grounded language learning from raw perceptual input.
papers.key_findings:
The PHON GRU model can predict visual features from phoneme sequences, performing between the non-sequential WORD SUM and sequential WORD GRU on image retrieval tasks.
Lower layers of PHON GRU are more sensitive to word boundaries (form), while higher layers are less sensitive, as shown by word boundary prediction accuracy decreasing from layer 1 to layer 3.
Word similarity correlations with human judgments increase from lower to higher layers, indicating that higher layers capture more semantic information.
Word similarity correlations with phonemic edit distance decrease from lower to higher layers, indicating that lower layers capture more form information.
Higher layers retain information over longer timescales, as shown by the average position of shared substrings in nearest neighbor sentences moving towards the beginning of the sentence in higher layers.
papers.limitation:
The model uses phonetic transcription rather than raw speech signal, which simplifies learning but is less naturalistic.
The visual input consists of high-level features from a pre-trained CNN, which contains ambiguity and noise compared to raw pixels.
future_direction: Apply models to acoustic speech signal coupled with visual input.
Investigate the nature of phonetic form information retained in higher layers and its analogy to human language representation.
papers.abstract:
We present a model of visually-grounded language learning based on stacked
gated recurrent neural networks which learns to predict visual features given
an image description in the form of a sequence of phonemes. The learning task
resembles that faced by human language learners who need to discover both
structure and meaning from noisy and ambiguous data across modalities. We show
that our model indeed learns to predict features of the visual context given
phonetically transcribed image descriptions, and show that it represents
linguistic information in a hierarchy of levels: lower layers in the stack are
comparatively more sensitive to form, whereas higher layers are more sensitive
to meaning.

papers.title: Slowness and Sparseness Lead to Place, Head-Direction, and Spatial-View Cells
papers.research_question: How can place cells, head-direction cells, and spatial-view cells self-organize from unsupervised learning on visual stimuli, and how does the movement pattern of the animal affect the type of cells that develop?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that place cells, head-direction cells, and spatial-view cells can emerge from an unsupervised learning model based on slowness (Slow Feature Analysis) and sparseness principles applied to visual input, with the cell type depending solely on the movement statistics of the simulated animal.
papers.conclusion: A purely sensory-driven unsupervised system can reproduce key properties of oriospatial cells (place, head-direction, spatial-view, and to some extent grid cells), with the output characteristics depending solely on the movement statistics.
papers.key_findings:
The same hierarchical SFA model can develop place cells, head-direction cells, or spatial-view cells depending on the movement pattern (relative rotational speed) of the simulated animal.
The SFA layer extracts a distributed, grid-like representation of position and orientation, which is then transformed into localized fields via sparse coding (ICA or competitive learning).
A mathematical analysis accurately predicts the output of the top SFA layer, showing that the slowest features correspond to Fourier-like basis functions in the configuration space.
Learning rate adaptation (LRA) based on vestibular-like signals allows concurrent learning of place cells and head-direction cells from the same movement statistics.
The model is purely sensory-driven and memoryless, demonstrating that complex spatial representations can form without path integration or explicit memory.
papers.limitation:
The model is memoryless and purely sensory-driven, so it cannot perform path integration.
The environment is static during training, which is not realistic.
The implementation of SFA (eigenvalue problem) and ICA (CuBICA) might not be biologically plausible.
future_direction: Extend the model to dynamic environments with changing variables (e.g., lighting).
Integrate other modalities such as olfactory cues.
Test the model's predictions experimentally, e.g., by manipulating movement statistics to influence cell invariance properties.
papers.abstract: We present a model for the self-organized formation of place cells, head-direction cells, and spatial-view cells in the hippocampal formation based on unsupervised learning on quasi-natural visual stimuli. The model comprises a hierarchy of Slow Feature Analysis (SFA) nodes, which were recently shown to reproduce many properties of complex cells in the early visual system []. The system extracts a distributed grid-like representation of position and orientation, which is transcoded into a localized place-field, head-direction, or view representation, by sparse coding. The type of cells that develops depends solely on the relevant input statistics, i.e., the movement pattern of the simulated animal. The numerical simulations are complemented by a mathematical analysis that allows us to accurately predict the output of the top SFA layer.

papers.title: Probing for Predicate Argument Structures in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: Do pretrained language models (PLMs) encode the argument structure of a predicate in its contextual representation? How are predicate senses and their argument structures encoded across layers, and how do they differ between verbal and nominal predicates and across languages?
papers.core_contribution: PLMs encode predicate argument structures in their contextual representations, with senses and rolesets encoded at different layers, and verbal and nominal predicates are represented differently. Integrating this knowledge improves SRL performance.
papers.conclusion: Probing PLMs for predicate argument structures reveals how they encode semantic information and provides insights that can be used to improve SRL systems.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode predicate argument structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate.
Predicate senses and their argument structures are encoded at different layers in PLMs.
Verbal and nominal predicate argument structures are represented differently across the layers of a PLM, making transfer between them non-trivial.
Multilingual PLMs encode predicate argument structure information similarly across English and Chinese.
Integrating predicate-argument structure knowledge into an SRL model via weighted averaging of layers and multi-task learning improves performance.
future_direction: cross-lingual transfer learning for SRL
using all layers of PLMs for SRL
papers.abstract: Thanks to the effectiveness and wide availability of modern pretrained language models (PLMs), recently proposed approaches have achieved remarkable results in dependencyand span-based, multilingual and cross-lingual Semantic Role Labeling (SRL). These results have prompted researchers to investigate the inner workings of modern PLMs with the aim of understanding how, where, and to what extent they encode information about SRL. In this paper, we follow this line of research and probe for predicate argument structures in PLMs. Our study shows that PLMs do encode semantic structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate, and also provides insights into the correlation between predicate senses and their structures, the degree of transferability between nominal and verbal structures, and how such structures are encoded across languages. Finally, we look at the practical implications of such insights and demonstrate the benefits of embedding predicate argument structure information into an SRL model.

papers.title: Deep Learning of Part-Based Representation of Data Using Sparse Autoencoders With Nonnegativity Constraints
papers.research_question: How can nonnegativity constraints in autoencoder training be used to learn part-based representations of data, and does this improve reconstruction and prediction performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a nonnegativity constraint algorithm (NCAE) for training autoencoders that learns part-based, sparse features, improving reconstruction quality and the prediction performance of deep networks.
papers.conclusion: Nonnegativity constraints in autoencoder training enable part-based representation learning, which improves reconstruction and classification performance in deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Nonnegativity constraints force autoencoders to learn features that capture a part-based representation of data.
NCAE achieves lower reconstruction error and better sparsity in hidden encoding compared to SAE and NMF.
A deep network pre-trained with NCAE achieves better classification accuracy than networks pre-trained with SAE, NNSAE, DAE, and DpAE on several datasets.
The learned features (receptive fields) are more interpretable, representing parts like strokes in digits or facial features.
The method works for both image and text data, extracting semantic features from documents.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate a new deep learning autoencoder network, trained by a nonnegativity constraint algorithm (nonnegativity-constrained autoencoder), that learns features that show part-based representation of data. The learning algorithm is based on constraining negative weights. The performance of the algorithm is assessed based on decomposing data into parts and its prediction performance is tested on three standard image data sets and one text data set. The results indicate that the nonnegativity constraint forces the autoencoder to learn features that amount to a part-based representation of data, while improving sparsity and reconstruction quality in comparison with the traditional sparse autoencoder and nonnegative matrix factorization. It is also shown that this newly acquired representation improves the prediction performance of a deep neural network.

papers.title: Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-conflicting facts are most enduring in language models and proposes a sparsification method to erase them while preserving task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers that knowledge-conflicting facts endure for many updates and cause inappropriate priming, and shows that their impact can be mitigated via multi-step sparse updates while preserving main task training.
papers.key_findings:
Facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while mundane and scrambled facts are forgotten more rapidly.
Knowledge-conflicting facts can prime how the model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts.
There is a sweet spot in fact novelty (between consistency and randomness) for memory durability.
The impact of knowledge-conflicting facts can be erased by multi-step sparse updates while preserving task performance.
future_direction: Extend the Outlandish dataset further
papers.abstract: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train? We investigate this question by injecting facts into LMs from a new probing dataset, "Outlandish", which is designed to permit the testing of a spectrum of different fact types. When studying how robust these memories are, there appears to be a sweet spot in the spectrum of fact novelty between consistency with world knowledge and total randomness, where the injected memory is the most enduring. Specifically we show that facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while prompts not conflicting with common knowledge (mundane), as well as scrambled prompts (randomly jumbled) are both forgotten much more rapidly. Further, knowledge-conflicting facts can "prime'' how the language model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts, showing their propensity for non-target generalization, while both mundane and randomly jumbled facts prime significantly less. Finally, we show that impacts of knowledge-conflicting facts in LMs, though they can be long lasting, can be largely erased by novel application of multi-step sparse updates, even while the training ability of the model is preserved. As such, this very simple procedure has direct implications for mitigating the effects of data poisoning in training.

papers.title: Pretrained Transformers as Universal Computation Engines
papers.research_question: We investigate the capability of a transformer pretrained on natural language to generalize to other modalities with minimal finetuning.
papers.core_contribution: A transformer pretrained on natural language can be effectively transferred to non-language tasks by freezing the self-attention and feedforward layers and only finetuning a small set of parameters, achieving strong performance.
papers.conclusion: Language-pretrained transformers can serve as universal computation engines, transferring effectively to non-language tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen Pretrained Transformer (FPT) achieves comparable performance to fully trained transformers on a variety of non-language tasks.
Language pretraining improves performance and compute efficiency over random initialization.
The transformer architecture (even randomly initialized) outperforms LSTM architectures on these tasks.
FPT converges faster than randomly initialized transformers.
The frozen attention layers learn to attend to semantically meaningful patterns in the data (e.g., in bit tasks).
future_direction: Investigating how to increase model expressiveness for better performance.
Exploring multimodal training/architectures.
Studying the role of different pretraining objectives and datasets.
papers.abstract: We investigate the capability of a transformer pretrained on natural language to generalize to other modalities with minimal finetuning -- in particular, without finetuning of the self-attention and feedforward layers of the residual blocks. We consider such a model, which we call a Frozen Pretrained Transformer (FPT), and study finetuning it on a variety of sequence classification tasks spanning numerical computation, vision, and protein fold prediction. In contrast to prior works which investigate finetuning on the same modality as the pretraining dataset, we show that pretraining on natural language can improve performance and compute efficiency on non-language downstream tasks. Additionally, we perform an analysis of the architecture, comparing the performance of a random initialized transformer to a random LSTM. Combining the two insights, we find language-pretrained transformers can obtain strong performance on a variety of non-language tasks.

papers.title: Interpreting CNN Knowledge via an Explanatory Graph
papers.research_question: How to interpret the knowledge hierarchy hidden inside a pre-trained CNN by learning an explanatory graph that disentangles part patterns from each filter and encodes their relationships.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to learn an explanatory graph that disentangles part patterns from each filter of a pre-trained CNN in an unsupervised manner, revealing the knowledge hierarchy and enabling transfer to part localization tasks.
papers.conclusion: The explanatory graph provides a concise and meaningful representation of the knowledge hierarchy inside CNNs, filtering out noisy activations and encoding part relationships, and demonstrates good transferability to part localization.
papers.key_findings:
The explanatory graph can disentangle distinct part patterns from each convolutional filter, where each graph node consistently represents the same object part across different images.
The learned part patterns have high semantic interpretability, with lower location instability compared to baseline methods.
The explanatory graph enables transfer of part patterns to part localization tasks, outperforming both unsupervised and supervised baselines.
The method is applicable to various CNN architectures, including VGG-16, residual networks, and VAE-GAN encoders.
papers.limitation: The explanatory graph is still a rough representation of the CNN, rather than an accurate reconstruction of the CNN knowledge.
papers.abstract: This paper learns a graphical model, namely an explanatory graph, which reveals the knowledge hierarchy hidden inside a pre-trained CNN. Considering that each filter in a conv-layer of a pre-trained CNN usually represents a mixture of object parts, we propose a simple yet efficient method to automatically disentangles different part patterns from each filter, and construct an explanatory graph. In the explanatory graph, each node represents a part pattern, and each edge encodes co-activation relationships and spatial relationships between patterns. More importantly, we learn the explanatory graph for a pre-trained CNN in an unsupervised manner, i.e., without a need of annotating object parts. Experiments show that each graph node consistently represents the same object part through different images. We transfer part patterns in the explanatory graph to the task of part localization, and our method significantly outperforms other approaches.

papers.title: Does my multimodal model learn cross-modal interactions? It’s harder to tell than you might think!
papers.research_question: Does the model actually use cross-modal interactions to improve performance, or is it mostly relying on unimodal signals?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EMAP, a diagnostic tool to project model predictions onto an additive space, and finds that for many multimodal tasks, cross-modal interactions are not being utilized by state-of-the-art models.
papers.conclusion: Recommends that future work on multimodal classification report the EMAP of their best model to better understand if cross-modal interactions are being used, and discusses hypotheses for why additive models are often sufficient.
papers.key_findings:
EMAP degrades performance on synthetic and balanced VQA tasks, confirming it can detect when cross-modal interactions are used.
For unbalanced multimodal classification tasks, EMAP often results in little to no performance degradation, indicating that even expressive models are not leveraging cross-modal interactions.
Performance improvements of interactive models over additive baselines are often not attributable to cross-modal interactions.
EMAP predictions are very similar to the original model's predictions for unbalanced tasks (agreement >95% in most cases).
For the T-VIS task, EMAP does degrade performance, suggesting that cross-modal interactions are being used in that specific case.
papers.limitation: EMAP, like model comparisons, provides insights about specific models on specific datasets but cannot fundamentally characterize the reasoning required by the task itself.
future_direction: Explore methods for understanding which datasets and instances can be rebalanced to require cross-modal interactions.
Estimate additive human baselines for comparison.
Improve unimodal modeling to enable better cross-modal interaction learning.
papers.abstract: Modeling expressive cross-modal interactions seems crucial in multimodal tasks, such as visual question answering. However, sometimes high-performing black-box algorithms turn out to be mostly exploiting unimodal signals in the data. We propose a new diagnostic tool, empirical multimodally-additive function projection (EMAP), for isolating whether or not cross-modal interactions improve performance for a given model on a given task. This function projection modifies model predictions so that cross-modal interactions are eliminated, isolating the additive, unimodal structure. For seven image+text classification tasks (on each of which we set new state-ofthe-art benchmarks), we find that, in many cases, removing cross-modal interactions results in little to no performance degradation. Surprisingly, this holds even when expressive models, with capacity to consider interactions, otherwise outperform less expressive models; thus, performance improvements, even when present, often cannot be attributed to consideration of cross-modal feature interactions. We hence recommend that researchers in multimodal machine learning report the performance not only of unimodal baselines, but also the EMAP of their best-performing model.

papers.title: Do Convolutional Neural Networks Learn Class Hierarchy?
papers.research_question: Do convolutional neural networks learn class hierarchy, and how does this hierarchy impact confusion patterns and feature learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Blocks, a visual-analytics system to reveal and analyze class hierarchy in CNNs, and shows that hierarchy-aware CNNs improve accuracy and convergence.
papers.conclusion: Class hierarchy impacts CNN learning and exploiting it improves CNN design and accuracy; visual-analytics methods help in understanding and improving CNNs.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs learn class hierarchy: early layers separate high-level groups, later layers separate fine-grained classes.
Class confusion patterns follow a hierarchical structure.
Hierarchy-aware CNNs accelerate convergence and reduce overfitting.
Blocks system helps identify data quality issues (overlapping class semantics, labeling issues, imbalanced distributions).
The system enables analysis of feature detectors and their development during training.
papers.limitation:
Blocks does not provide information about layer connectivity and visualizes layer responses independently, hindering inspection of how feature detectors develop across layers.
Blocks offers limited possibilities to monitor the training process.
future_direction: Study how class similarity structures influence other types of large-scale classifiers and generalize findings to domains other than image classification.
papers.abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) currently achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in image classification. With a growing number of classes, the accuracy usually drops as the possibilities of confusion increase. Interestingly, the class confusion patterns follow a hierarchical structure over the classes. We present visual-analytics methods to reveal and analyze this hierarchy of similar classes in relation with CNN-internal data. We found that this hierarchy not only dictates the confusion patterns between the classes, it furthermore dictates the learning behavior of CNNs. In particular, the early layers in these networks develop feature detectors that can separate high-level groups of classes quite well, even after a few training epochs. In contrast, the latter layers require substantially more epochs to develop specialized feature detectors that can separate individual classes. We demonstrate how these insights are key to significant improvement in accuracy by designing hierarchy-aware CNNs that accelerate model convergence and alleviate overfitting. We further demonstrate how our methods help in identifying various quality issues in the training data.

papers.title: Contextual Gradient Interference: A Novel Mechanism for Knowledge Retention and Adaptability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in large language models by enabling knowledge retention while adapting to new tasks through a gradient-based mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism, a dual-gradient framework that dynamically partitions parameter updates to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and enhance knowledge retention and adaptability in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism successfully addresses catastrophic forgetting by balancing knowledge preservation and task adaptation, demonstrating improved performance and scalability in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
The CGI mechanism improves accuracy, reduces perplexity, and enhances retention scores across various tasks.
It outperforms baseline models in retention scores for sequential learning tasks.
The model shows adaptability to variable contexts, though performance declines with increased complexity in multi-hop reasoning.
Scalability tests show accuracy plateaus beyond 100GB dataset size, with training time increasing non-linearly.
The model is robust to noisy inputs but accuracy decreases with higher noise levels.
papers.limitation:
Increased computational overhead associated with gradient decomposition and real-time masking
Reliance on auxiliary loss functions requiring careful hyperparameter calibration
Sensitivity to input quality under noisy conditions
future_direction: Investigating alternative methods for gradient decomposition, such as sparse or low-rank approximations
Incorporating reinforcement learning paradigms to dynamically adjust masking parameters based on task feedback
Exploring integration with emerging architectures, such as sparse attention or memory-augmented transformers
papers.abstract: Addressing the challenge of catastrophic forgetting in large-scale neural architectures requires innovative solutions that enable models to retain prior knowledge while adapting to new tasks. The proposed Contextual Gradient Interference mechanism introduces a dual-gradient framework designed to partition parameter updates dynamically, ensuring stability for previously learned information while facilitating effective task-specific adaptations. By leveraging real-time gradient analysis and masking strategies, the mechanism mitigates interference and promotes efficient learning across sequential tasks. The integration of this approach within the Falcon model, a state-of-the-art open-source language model, demonstrated significant improvements in knowledge retention, task adaptability, and robustness under varying conditions, including noisy inputs and increasing dataset sizes. Quantitative evaluations across multiple benchmarks revealed enhanced accuracy, lower perplexity, and improved memory retention compared to existing methodologies. The scalability of the approach was further validated through its computational efficiency and performance consistency over extended training cycles. Additional experiments highlighted the ability of the model to handle multi-hop reasoning and sequential tasks with complex contextual dependencies, showcasing the versatility of the proposed mechanism. An ablation study reinforced the significance of key components, such as gradient masking and decomposition, in achieving the observed performance gains. Results also revealed areas for potential optimization, including computational trade-offs and sensitivity to hyperparameter configurations. The study advances the understanding of gradient-based learning strategies and their critical role in optimizing neural networks for dynamic and large-scale tasks. Through its novel contributions, the mechanism establishes a foundation for enhancing the stability, adaptability, and efficiency of language model training, making it an invaluable tool for future developments in machine learning.

papers.title: Taming Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models handle knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and contextual information, and can we design a method to steer them towards either source without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory in attention heads and proposes JUICE, a test-time attention intervention method that steers LMs toward either parametric or contextual knowledge without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: JUICE sets a new state-of-the-art for handling knowledge conflicts, offering robust generalization across domains and conflict types, and is supported by theoretical analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit inconsistent behaviors under different degrees of knowledge conflict, challenging the notion of exclusive 'memory heads' and 'context heads'.
Combining individually effective interventions can lead to counteracting effects due to superposition.
JUICE achieves state-of-the-art performance in steering LMs towards parametric or contextual knowledge across diverse datasets and models.
JUICE is effective even with a very small head identification set (e.g., 4 samples).
The dual-run design of JUICE mitigates superposition effects and outperforms single-run interventions.
